articles.title: RNC chair predicts ‘big surprises’ for midterm elections
articles.summary: "We have been building the momentum over the last 30 days with the president on the road rallying the base," Gruters said.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — With less than 24 hours until Election Day and control of Congress at stake, Republican National Convention Chairman Joe Gruters believes some "big surprises" are coming.

Democrats projected to win back Congress: Decision Desk HQ

While NewsNation's polling partner, Decision Desk HQ , currently projects Democrats to win back both chambers of Congress, Gruters said he expects his party to emerge victorious in the races needed to prevent that from happening.

"We have been building the momentum over the last 30 days with the president on the road rallying the base ," Gruters said. "I expect our base to turn out heavily tomorrow, like we normally do."

In one of the most consequential races for control of the Senate, DDHQ polling data shows Michigan Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed holds a slight edge over Republican Mike Rogers.

Gruters, however, said he expects Rogers to win and called him one of the Republicans' best Senate candidates. This comes as Rep. Haley Stevens , the Democrat who narrowly lost Michigan's Senate primary to El-Sayed, endorsed Rogers in a surprise move Sunday .

Gruters added that he believes Stevens' support will have "a massive impact" on voters and that "she's just one of many Democrats who thinks El-Sayed is too radical and reckless for that Michigan seat."

articles.body:
Vice President Vance is hitting the campaign trail in New York and Ohio on Monday, making a final push for Republicans with the midterms just one day away.

He will first rally voters in Rome, N.Y., alongside GOP House hopeful Anthony Constantino, who is competing in a district President Trump carried by 21 points in 2024. Constantino is running against Democrat Blake Gendebien for New York's 21st Congressional District seat being vacated by Rep. Elise Stefanik (R).

Vance will then travel to Swanton, Ohio, where Republicans are fighting to hold onto a key Senate seat. Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) is locked in a tight reelection battle with former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D). Decision Desk HQ rates the race as favoring Brown.

His remarks in New York are scheduled to begin at 10:45 a.m. EST, followed by the trip to Ohio, expected around 1:05 p.m. EST.

articles.title: Carville rips Stevens over Rogers endorsement: ‘Your political career is over’
articles.summary: Democratic Strategist James Carville said Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) sold her soul in endorsing former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) for Senate in Michigan over her primary rival, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed. The strategist took to YouTube to disavow Stevens for coming out against El-Sayed in a battleground race that could decide control of the Senate. Carville…
articles.body:
Democratic Strategist James Carville said Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) sold her soul in endorsing former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) for Senate in Michigan over her primary rival, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.

The strategist took to YouTube to disavow Stevens for coming out against El-Sayed in a battleground race that could decide control of the Senate. Carville said Stevens’s political career is over and panned her for siding with Republicans, who he said are committing “treason of the highest level.”

“You got to put some kind of a price on yourself, or some kind of goddamn self-pride. But your political career is over,” Carville said.

Stevens came out in support of Rogers — a staunch supporter of President Trump, whom she has strongly spoken out against in the past — after El-Sayed disinvited her from a campaign stop over the weekend. Stevens said in an appearance on CNN on Sunday night that the Democratic nominee was injecting “anger” into the race, and she has taken issue with El-Sayed’s stance on Israel.

Carville likened Stevens’s move to Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.), who has often crossed his party and voted with Republicans, particularly on issues related to Israel.

“I think El-Sayed offered her one cheeseburger and Rogers offered her two cheeseburgers, and in the spirit of John Fetterman, s—, gimme another cheeseburger and I’ll give you my soul,” Carville said. “I mean, lady, if you’re going to sell your soul, you got to get more for it than a f—ing cheeseburger, OK.”

Stevens said Sunday that she was putting country over party in her endorsement of Rogers and that she still wants to see Democrats take the Senate majority. She has been widely panned across the Democratic landscape for the perceived betrayal, while Trump applauded the legislator and said he would welcome her to the GOP.

Carville said Republicans will treat Stevens poorly if she joins the GOP, while Democrats won’t associate with her at all.

“If you think that these Republicans are going to treat you as anything other than what they view you as, and that is, let me just break the news to you — a used condom,” Carville said. “The Democrats don’t even think you’re worth a used condom, but that’s about where you are. You made your bed, sleep in it. You s— in your mess kit, eat it.”

The Hill has reached out to Stevens’s congressional office for comment.

articles.title: Judge tosses case against ex-FBI officials accused of lying to Congress about Hunter Biden investigation
articles.summary: A federal judge dismissed the case against two FBI officials in the Hunter Biden probe, accusing Trump and Kash Patel of directing a "rush job."
articles.body: A federal judge tossed criminal charges against two former FBI officials accused of lying to Congress about the Hunter Biden investigation Monday, delivering a blistering rebuke of the prosecution and accusing the Trump administration's Justice Department of weaponizing the justice system. U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui dismissed the criminal complaint against former FBI officials Nikki Cole Floris and Bradley Benavides from the bench, sharply criticizing the government's handling of the prosecution. "What has transpired here cannot be described as anything other than weaponization," Faruqui said, describing the case as a "rush job" directed by President Donald Trump and FBI Director Kash Patel. The case stemmed from allegations that the officials lied to Congress about their knowledge of Hunter Biden’s laptop and the bureau’s handling of investigations involving him ahead of the 2020 presidential election. EX-FBI OFFICIALS ARRESTED IN HUNTER BIDEN LAPTOP PROBE AS TESTIMONY COMES UNDER SCRUTINY The ruling capped a series of hearings in which Faruqui questioned the government's decision to pursue the case through a criminal complaint rather than a grand jury indictment and blasted prosecutors for attempting to add another charge without first securing judicial approval. Republicans have long accused the FBI of improperly handling information about Hunter Biden ahead of the 2020 presidential election, alleging that political bias influenced the bureau's decisions. Prosecutors alleged that Floris and Benavides made false statements during congressional interviews in 2023 about what they knew and did that were contradicted by internal FBI communications and witness accounts. During a preliminary hearing last week, Faruqui blasted prosecutors for filing an unsigned, unsworn criminal complaint seeking to add obstruction charges without first obtaining judicial approval. Faruqui struck the revised complaint from the record, forcing prosecutors to proceed on their original allegations that the former officials lied to Congress. FBI CO-DEPUTY DIRECTOR ANDREW BAILEY RESIGNS AFTER YEAR IN ROLE The judge questioned why prosecutors had bypassed standard procedures, while defense attorneys pointed out that the revised complaint also softened the government's original allegations about the officials' involvement in Hunter Biden investigations. Faruqui, who was appointed a U.S. magistrate judge in 2020, has previously sharply criticized federal prosecutors handling cases under the Trump administration. He apologized to the suspect accused of plotting an assassination attempt against Trump at the White House Correspondents’ Association Dinner. JUDGE WHO APOLOGIZED TO ACCUSED WOULD-BE TRUMP ASSASSIN LIGHTS UP DOJ IN HUNTER BIDEN FBI CASE "To me, it’s extremely disturbing that he was put in five-point restraints, a person with no criminal history. It’s troubling," said Faruqui, referring to suspect Cole Allen's jail treatment in May. "I never heard of one Jan. 6 defendant who was put in five-point restraints or in a safe cell. If the only way to keep him safe is the most punitive thing, that’s a problem." Faruqui also previously clashed with federal prosecutors in Washington over Trump administration law-enforcement surge cases, accusing U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s office of overreaching by bringing some matters in federal court that he said belonged in local court. articles.title: MAGA sold us masculinity. So why are they scared of everyone?
articles.summary: Marine veteran Joslin Joseph argues that Republican fear-mongering regarding transgender and Muslim Americans exploits the anxieties of young men who feel increasingly alienated in modern society.
articles.body:
Like any patriotic red-blooded American male, I spend a lot of time watching football. I will spend Saturdays overreacting to Ohio State losses or non-blowout wins and spend Sundays on the emotional roller coaster called the New York Giants. I also have NFL Sunday Ticket and all those streaming services so I can see plenty of other games as well. It means every two years, I get bombarded with political campaigns. Sometimes, I hit the mute button or flip to another game. And sometimes, I watch them and wonder the exact same thought every time.

Are MAGA men scared of everyone? And by everyone, I mean everyone who is even slightly different than they are. Let’s start with the two most obvious ones. Transgender Americans and Muslim Americans. Republicans are selling Americans that the cause of their problems isn’t the Iran war, tariffs or corporate greed. Nope, they have poured in over $180 million to warn you about transgender people trying to have a normal life in this country.

I often wonder how MAGA men run into so many transgender people that they are scared to death of them. I am a California liberal who was born and raised in New Jersey and went to Harvard. I think I have met only three transgender people in my life. None of those people turned me into a transgender person. They just turned me into a friend.

The same hysteria has been leveled at Muslim-Americans. Vote Democrat and you will find yourself living under Sharia law. I mean, it didn’t happen when they said it would happen under President Barack Obama’s eight-year administration. It hasn’t happened yet in New York City despite the warnings about Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Living in Anaheim, Calif., I can go to the part of town called Little Arabia. No jihadists but plenty of great places to eat.

And yet MAGA commercials insist that this time, if we elect this candidate (Abdul El-Sayed for U.S. Senate in Michigan), the dam holding back Islamists will break and this country will be overrun. In the 25 years since 9/11, we have been inundated with anti-Muslim rhetoric which works against efforts to identify and prevent Islamic extremism. If you treat everyone like a criminal, it will be harder to find the actual criminals.

In 2024, a lot of young men voted for Donald Trump. There are plenty of reasons for this, but masculinity was one of them. The overall feeling is that it is hard to be a man in America. Before you break out the small violins, know that it might not be that bad, but it is definitely not that good. The suicide rate of men is high and highest among white men . Getting married and having kids is more of a challenge. Buying a home is harder. And more young women than men are getting college degrees which means they might make more money.

Now, is this the fault of feminists, wokeism, communists, and Democrats? Not quite, but liberals really didn’t help. It seemed that every conversation on social media about toxic masculinity would devolve into people saying that all masculinity is toxic. Always choose the bear. People would rail about the patriarchy to guys who were just struggling to get through life. And who could forget how even corporations lectured us on being men. Remember that Gillette ad ? You would think that the Republicans would offer better solutions, right?

Instead, we had right-wing influencers, podcasters, and the so-called manosphere focused on the wrong things. How many times were we told to get mad over comic book characters, women (especially Black women) in movies or TV shows, women’s sports that we don’t watch, and a myriad of other trivial things. We were inundated with pick me girls, Only Fans creators, superficial dating apps, and bros selling us on focusing on trivial things. Comparing yourself to other men based on the coffee you drink or the type of meat you eat.

But in that noise there was attention. And Republicans jumped on it and said they understood what men were dealing with. Now, we know that a lot of men turned to the Republicans because it appealed more to their beliefs on manhood. But in this runup to the midterms, I have to ask. Is falling for fear-mongering part of being a man? Actively seeking out people who are different from you and finding commonalities with them ensures peace and stability. And that is what this country needs.

And the polling shows that’s what young men want too . We need men in this country to learn to adapt not just financially, but socially to changes so that they can thrive. Teaching them to live in fear only puts them behind the eight ball and ensures they will be left behind. Franklin Roosevelt famously said, “the only thing to fear is fear itself.” MAGA Republicans are telling men to fear everyone. Which mindset is manlier?

Joslin Joseph is a recipient of the 2025 Military Reporters and Editors award for Best Commentary / Opinion. A graduate of Harvard and Ohio State, he is a Marine veteran who served in Iraq. He currently lives in Anaheim, Calif.

articles.title: Taking a ballot selfie? It may be prohibited in your state
articles.summary: Not every state supports taking a photo with your ballot.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Whether you’re voting for the first time or your 50th, casting a ballot on Election Day can feel monumental, so much so that you want to take a photo to capture the moment.

Depending on where you are, that may not be allowed.

States have varying rules on “ballot selfies,” according to the National Conference of State Legislatures .

In Michigan , voters can take a photo of their ballot in the booth, but they cannot hold up the ballot for a selfie, officials say. Selfies are allowed and “encouraged” outside the polling location.

Oklahoma law prohibits a voter from sharing how they voted while inside the election enclosure. Officials say voters in the state can take a photo of their marked ballot but cannot share it with someone or on social media until they’ve left the enclosure.

Alabama allows voters to photograph their ballot “as long as they do not disclose the content of any other voter’s ballot or disrupt the voting process.”

Maryland also allows voters to take a photo of their marked ballot.

Voters in other states do not have the same opportunity.

“Wireless communications devices” aren’t allowed in a room where voting is happening, and images and sound can’t be recorded within 100 feet of a voting station, according to Texas election officials.

While there is no law that stops a voter from taking a picture or recording video at a Minnesota polling place, the Secretary of State’s office discourages it. Recording a marked ballot “could violate” state law as well.

Others prohibiting ballot selfies, according to an NCSL analysis, include Nevada, South Dakota, Wisconsin, Missouri, Louisiana, Mississippi, South Carolina, North Carolina, New Jersey, New York, Massachusetts, Alaska, and Ohio.

Before you snap a selfie with your ballot, be sure to check with local election regulations. There may be signs at your polling place warning you against the practice.

articles.title: Nate Silver: Latest preelection polling shows ‘blue tsunami’ on horizon
articles.summary: Political analyst Nate Silver predicted Sunday that a “blue tsunami” is on the horizon. Silver, a political forecaster and statistician, reacted to the newest slate of polling from The New York Times and Siena University showing Democrats leading their GOP opponents in key Senate contests. “NYT/Siena released their presumably final set of polls this evening,…
articles.body:
Political analyst Nate Silver predicted Sunday that a “blue tsunami” is on the horizon.

Silver, a political forecaster and statistician, reacted to the newest slate of polling from The New York Times and Siena University showing Democrats leading their GOP opponents in key Senate contests.

“NYT/Siena released their presumably final set of polls this evening, and they showed what can only be described as fantastic numbers for Democrats, putting them ahead — sometimes narrowly, sometimes not — in basically every Senate battleground and in the associated governor’s races, including in Texas,” Silver wrote in his newsletter , noting that much of the polling is in line with his modeling.

The final round of polls released by The Times on Sunday showed Democrats leading in many of the key Senate battlegrounds, including in Michigan by 11 percentage points, in Texas by 7, Kansas by 5 and Alaska by 1. Silver said the poll’s results were close but not within his model’s “weird” territory, adding that the data suggests Democrats are likely to take the Senate.

“Democrats could actually absorb a modest-sized polling error and perhaps still prevail given the latest round of surveys,” Silver wrote.

With less than a day before Election Day, Democrats hold the edge in the polls. They are poised to win or seriously compete in historically red states, including South Carolina, Kansas and Iowa.

Silver pointed out that even if Democrats lose a handful of these red state races, they won’t necessarily be complaining.

“Even if Democrats were to lose a couple of these races — and there’s actually some bad news for them here in Alaska, I think — absolutely no Democrat is going to complain if they only flip the top five races in this chart, especially if it comes along with the Texas governorship,” Silver wrote.

The forecaster said while his operation typically does not focus closely on single polls, the Times/Siena poll has pushed his model’s forecast of Democrats’ chances of winning the Senate majority into the 80 percent range. He said while the poll has produced favorable numbers for Democrats this cycle, that is taken into account.

“Although the model trusts the NYT/Siena polls a lot — they’re among our more highly-rated pollsters — it does adjust every survey firm’s numbers for house effects. In other words, it knows that NYT/Siena has tended to have good numbers for Democrats this cycle, and that’s priced into its forecasts,” Silver wrote.

articles.title: Haley Stevens endorses Mike Rogers over Abdul El-Sayed. Who has a better chance of winning Michigan's marquee Senate battle?
articles.summary: Rep. Haley Stevens, whom Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeated in Michigan's Democratic primary, endorsed Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday. Here's where the Senat...
articles.body:
On Election Day, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers will face off in what may be the marquee battle of the 2026 midterms: the race to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters in Michigan.

It's a contest that could decide which party controls the U.S. Senate.

Democrats currently hold 47 Senate seats, including two independents who caucus with them. They need 51 to win back the chamber. (A 50-50 split would give Vice President JD Vance the tiebreaking vote.) Polls suggest that flipping four Republican seats is very possible , but Democrats are also playing defense in Georgia, New Hampshire and Michigan. The Great Lakes State looks like the closest of the three.

Democrats are pinning their hopes on El-Sayed , an unapologetic 42-year-old progressive who's pushing policies such as Medicare for All and ending U.S. military aid to Israel; who's willing to confront his critics and his own party's establishment; and who's vying to become America's first Muslim senator.

Republicans have handed the reins to Rogers , a 63-year-old former congressman who lost an extremely close Senate race to Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin two years ago, and who has since broken with President Trump on tariffs and the war in Iran.

The race has been rocked by several controversies, and the biggest came Sunday, two days before the election. Rep. Haley Stevens, the Democrat El-Sayed narrowly defeated in the primary, endorsed Rogers after the two worshipped together at Perfecting Church in Detroit.

"Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away," Stevens said in a video. "And he's right. And that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today."

Stevens had said days earlier that she would vote for El-Sayed, and the two were due to appear together Sunday for the first time since August. That plan collapsed after she called on him to condemn an outside group's ad tying U.S. support for Israel to grocery prices. His campaign then asked her to stay away , NBC News reported.

Defending her stance, Stevens told CNN on Sunday the decision was a "weight off my shoulders" and said she had decided to switch allegiances because El-Sayed had been getting "angrier and angrier" throughout the campaign.

When Stevens announced her change in support for Rogers, she maintained that she was "still a very proud Democrat." Michigan's Democratic Party chair, Curtis Hertel, fumed over the decision in a Sunday post on X , writing, "Congresswoman Stevens is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future."

Trump told a rally in Iowa on Sunday that he'd "love" Stevens to join the Republican Party and said she'd been "very brave" to endorse Rogers.

Rep. Debbie Dingell, who helped arrange the event, told the AP before the endorsement that she had called it off. "I'm the one who pulled it because it had become way too distracting," she said.

"I would rather not distract from the key issues of this campaign," El-Sayed said Saturday . He attended a different Detroit church Sunday with Dingell and other Democrats, and did not address the dispute there, the AP reported. Stevens's longtime chief of staff resigned after the church visit, and more staff were expected to leave, the AP reported, citing a person familiar with the matter.

On Sunday, El-Sayed spoke with reporters before a unity event with other Democrats and reacted to Stevens's endorsement, saying, "At the end of the day, I actually don't think about Haley Stevens."

"This is a state of 10 million people who deserve a lot better from their government. I'm a lot more focused on the 9,999,998 that are not the ones you guys are talking about," El-Sayed said, referring to Stevens and Rogers.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer wrote on social media on Sunday that Stevens's reversal was a "despicable betrayal."

Jason Turkish, Stevens's fiancé, said last week that he would vote for Rogers because of El-Sayed's criticism of Israel's conduct in Gaza.

"Every time [El-Sayed] talks about genocide, Jews get death threats," Turkish, a Michigan lawyer and registered Democrat, claimed Oct. 28 at a Rogers campaign event . "We have never seen a candidate for U.S. Senate act so recklessly toward the safety of Jews in the community as we have seen from Abdul."

Further raising the stakes is the fact that Michigan couldn't be more purple, having swung to Trump in 2016, then Democrat Joe Biden in 2020, then back to Trump in 2024 — always by slim margins.

Here's everything you need to know about the Michigan Senate contest.

Who's winning? Here's what the polls say.

Twelve polls have been conducted in October. Eleven of them have shown El-Sayed with leads ranging from 1 to 7 percentage points . New surveys from both CBS Detroit and CNN give El-Sayed a 7-point lead. The only recent poll to show Rogers ahead (by 2 points) was sponsored by a group affiliated with the former congressman . All of those polls were taken before Stevens's endorsement.

To close the gap on Election Day, Rogers has been reaching out to two groups who backed Stevens over El-Sayed in the primary: Black and Jewish Democrats.

In August, Stevens won a majority of Michigan's large counties with significant Black populations by an average of 8.5 percentage points . She also won Detroit with more than 60% of the vote, making El-Sayed the first Michigan Democrat since 2018 to win a statewide primary without winning the state's largest city.

Some members of Michigan's Jewish community also gravitated toward Stevens because El-Sayed has called the war in Gaza a "genocide" and accused Democrats who refuse to do the same of lacking the courage necessary "to stand up to Donald Trump."

"Killing tens of thousands of people makes you pretty damn evil," El-Sayed told CNN in April . "It's not how evil is this one versus that one. Hamas: evil. Israeli government: evil. We can say both."

It remains to be seen whether Rogers's outreach will pay off; he's also targeting more reliable Republican constituencies such as the nearly 4 million Michiganders ages 50 and older. So far, polls suggest that El-Sayed's strategy — trying to maximize his support among anti-establishment voters, Arab Americans and young voters — has put him ahead in the polls.

But the polls have overestimated El-Sayed before. In the run-up to August's primary, several surveys showed El-Sayed with a double-digit lead over Stevens. The race ended up being much closer than expected, with El-Sayed edging Stevens by less than 1 percentage point .

El-Sayed's background has also made him the target of persistent attacks from Republicans, with Trump going so far as to call him a "jihadist" and accuse him of being "on the side of the terrorists."

Vice President JD Vance recently said El-Sayed had "zero attachment" to the United States. El-Sayed is a U.S. citizen who was born and raised in Michigan. Rogers has claimed without evidence that El-Sayed has supported the Muslim Brotherhood, one of the Arab world's oldest and most influential Islamist groups.

In a recent exchange at a town hall with a critic who asked him whether he denounced the Muslim Brotherhood, El-Sayed highlighted what he called the "implicit" suggestion in the question: the assumption that he'll have "dual loyalties" because of his faith.

"I'm not running to be a Muslim senator," he said. "I'm running for the U.S. Senate and happen to be Muslim."

After Trump referred to El-Sayed as " Mohammed " — his middle name — the Democrat responded in what has become his signature pugnacious style.

"I don't care how he pronounces my name," El-Sayed said during a rally in Grand Rapids on Oct. 25. "Because he can just go on and call me 'senator' after November. I will be Senator Mohamed to you, bro."

Meanwhile, El-Sayed has campaigned with Hasan Piker , a Marxist streamer whom other Democrats have called antisemitic and even anti-American .

"If perfectly inoffensive won elections, then Donald Trump would never have been president," El-Sayed said in April when reporters questioned his choice of allies.

An independent left-wing group affiliated with Piker's uncle, commentator Cenk Uygur, also recently released an ad linking U.S. support for Israel to high grocery prices. The ad shows two parents shopping for their kids' lunch items; the mom tells the dad to put a carton of eggs back on the shelf.

"They don't like eggs anymore?" the dad asks.

"No, they like eggs," the mom answers. "But we have to set that $7 aside for killing Palestinians."

Some Democrats and Republicans have urged El-Sayed to denounce the content of the ad rather than just distancing himself from it.

"That has nothing to do with our campaign," El-Sayed said of the ad. "It's certainly not what I want to be talking about right now."

El-Sayed, 42, was born on Halloween 1984 in Rochester Hills, Mich. — a northern suburb of Detroit. His parents were immigrants from Egypt, and his first language was Arabic. He captained his high school's wrestling, football and lacrosse teams, then continued to play club lacrosse at the University of Michigan, where he majored in biology and political science.

El-Sayed went on to study medicine at Michigan, Oxford University (as a Rhodes Scholar) and Columbia University, where he received his MD. Before politics, he pursued a career in public health epidemiology as a tenure-track professor, and later led the Detroit health department.

In 2017, El-Sayed, then just 32, resigned as Detroit's health director to run for governor. He said at the time he was inspired by his work on the Flint water crisis . He was endorsed by prominent progressives — Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez — but lost the Democratic primary to Gretchen Whitmer by more than 20 percentage points.

After a stint as Wayne County health director, El-Sayed decided to try again in 2026. He has since become the most prominent Democratic insurgent to channel left-wing disillusionment with politics and outrage over Israel's actions in Gaza to win his party's nomination in a state where more moderate candidates typically prevail. His argument is that even in so-called purple states such as Michigan, Democrats have a better shot at success when they pick buzzy, big-swing progressives over safe, "electable" incrementalists.

Rogers was born in Livingston County, Mich., in 1963. He earned a bachelor's degree in criminal justice and sociology from Adrian College in 1985 before joining the Army. After four years of military service, Rogers joined the FBI as a special agent based in Chicago. His work with federal law enforcement focused on countering organized crime and public corruption. Rogers began his political career in 1994, when he was elected to a seat in the Michigan state legislature. He served for six years before launching his first bid for Congress.

Rogers was elected to the House of Representatives in one of the closest races of the 2000 election cycle, defeating Democrat Dianne Byrum by just 111 votes . During his 14-year tenure in the House, Rogers was a key conservative voice on national security and intelligence issues. He spent four years as chairman of the powerful House Intelligence Committee, much of that time focused on what he describes as "the economic and national security danger posed by China."

Rogers left Congress in 2015 and quickly began a career in media. He hosted a daily syndicated radio show called Something to Think About with Mike Rogers and worked as a commentator for CNN.

Rogers returned to run for the Senate in 2024. Roughly six months after that loss, he announced his plan to run again in 2026.

Rogers is a conservative Republican on most issues — including abortion, immigration and transgender rights — but his opinion on Trump has shifted through the years. Over the past few weeks, Rogers has retreated from his early support for the president on two key issues: calling for Trump to end the "tariff war" with Canada and saying the conflict in Iran should also "end quickly."

articles.title: The Trump era is over
articles.summary: Cause of death: political suicide.
articles.body:
When the history of the 2026 midterm elections is written, the most remembered political advertisement will be Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s (R) commercial starring the mother of his opponent, Dr. Amy Acton (D).

Acton was called a “ liar ” by her mother, who fled the state along with her abusive husband after he was charged with raping Acton, his stepdaughter. Removed from her home by the state of Ohio, Acton had not seen her mother since 1978.

Ramaswamy’s advertisement generated an immediate political backlash. Ohio’s Republican governor, Mike DeWine, urged Ramaswamy to take it off the air . Local businesses canceled events featuring the beleaguered Republican candidate. And the Cleveland Plain Dealer endorsed Acton, saying that Ramaswamy had “ crossed a line .”

But President Trump and JD Vance doubled down in backing Ramaswamy. Trump said that if a candidate’s mother called her daughter a liar, that was political “ gold .” Vance complained that Republicans should “stop whining” about Ramaswamy’s tactics, adding, “Politics is a tough business.” After spending $1 million , the Ramaswamy campaign took the controversial ad off the air .

But something bigger than the misadventures of one Republican candidate is at work here. In Kansas, a pastor has a chance to win a Senate seat Democrats have not won since 1932 . And in Texas, a state senator and seminarian, has consistently run ahead in the polls, giving Democrats a chance to win a U.S. Senate seat in a state where the party has not won one since 1988 .

Some have said that only Trump could have gotten away with running an ad like Ramaswamy’s. After all, when Trump first appeared on the political scene many of his devoted followers admired him for rejecting “ political correctness ” and saying things other conventional politicians would not.

But this is wrong. Today, the stench of political death has repelled even Trump’s most devoted followers. On the campaign trail, Trump speaks to arenas filled with empty seats . And in the words of Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), those who show up are subjected to two hours of “ senile babbling .”

Even a dozen Catholic bishops who were filmed praying over Trump distanced themselves from him . Milwaukee Archbishop Jeffrey S. Grob called the meeting a mistake and apologized for “the pain I caused.” Denver Archbishop James R. Golka said it “was never my intention” for the encounter to be seen as an endorsement.

Americans are profoundly dissatisfied with Trump’s performance, including high gas and grocery prices, the killing of innocent citizens on urban streets, the mass deportation of migrants who have raised families in the U.S. and are a vital engine of economic growth and starting a war with Iran. This runs contrary to Trump’s 2024 promises to bring down costs, deport only migrant criminals and never start another foreign war.

The sense of betrayal is so pervasive that Trump’s job approval ratings have fallen to historic lows .

Rather than solving the problems that concern Americans most, Trump is building a ballroom and an arch , littering the White House with gold and defacing the Reflecting Pool on the National Mall. Barack Obama likened Trump’s gold-littered White House to Saddam Hussein’s opening a Cheesecake Factory.

The path forward to addressing the problems Trump has created is unclear. Some want to deal with the healthcare crisis by creating a Medicare for All option. Potential job losses caused by artificial intelligence and how to regulate it are issues where most agree something must be done, but the solutions are unclear. Dealing with inadequate housing and covering the cost of childcare involve differing approaches. And the Iran War is akin to an unsolvable puzzle where a lasting peace deal might be impossible.

But what is clear is that Americans are demanding an end to the anything-goes rhetoric and want leaders they can admire. Two past presidents — one a Democrat, the other a Republican — set examples that resonate today.

After the stench of Watergate, Jimmy Carter promised a government that was “as competent, as compassionate, as good” as the American people.

Carter’s successor, Ronald Reagan, was also widely admired. New York’s Democratic governor, Mario Cuomo, once said of Reagan, “By his personal conduct when he’s shot, when he’s told he has cancer, when he goes to Normandy — the way he’s deported himself has been a moral instruction to my children.”

Baron de Montesquieu once argued that virtue is “the spring which sets the republican government in motion.” This year, the competitive races run by Democrats Adam Hamilton in Kansas and James Talarico in Texas are signs of an emerging new era where partisanship is cast aside in favor of virtuous leaders who set a high moral example and are role models the rest of us can admire.

The springs of government may be back in motion, but the Trump Era is over. Cause of death: political suicide.

John Kenneth White is a professor emeritus at The Catholic University of America who writes on Substack . His latest book, coauthored with Matthew R. Kerbel, is titled “ Democracy on the Edge: The Trump Elections and the Future of American Politics.”

articles.title: Judge dismisses case against ex-FBI agents accused on lying to Congress in Hunter Biden investigation
articles.summary: A judge dismissed a criminal complaint against a pair of former FBI officials accused of lying to Congress about what they knew about the Hunter Biden investigation, a person familiar with the matter confirmed to NBC News.
articles.body: A federal judge on Monday dismissed a criminal complaint against a pair of former FBI officials accused of lying to Congress during its investigation of Hunter Biden. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui found the government had failed to show probable cause that Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides had lied to lawmakers about what they knew about the investigation into Hunter Biden’s laptop. Data from the abandoned computer later led to successful criminal charges against former President Joe Biden’s son. The case was brought by criminal complaint rather than being presented to a federal grand jury in Washington, where jurors have been skeptical of politically-tinged cases against purported Trump enemies, most recently rejecting the attempted indictment of Cassidy Hutchinson. The complaint alleged that the duo lied about their roles on the Foreign Influence Task Force and “about their roles in the FBI’s Hunter Biden investigations” while testifying before the House Judiciary Committee in 2023. The dismissal came after an FBI agent testified at a preliminary hearing last week that he was concerned the investigation, which had been directed by FBI Director Kash Patel, would be viewed as “political.” He also acknowledged a prosecutor on the case had acknowledged the criminal complaint was flawed in a telephone call last week. That prosecutor, Carlton Davis — a top aide to the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, Jeanine Pirro — is a former Republican Hill staffer who was also involved in the failed indictment of six sitting members of Congress over a social media video that President Donald Trump disfavored. The case could theoretically still move forward if the Justice Department were able to convince federal grand jurors of probable cause, but that outcome seems unlikely given Faruqui’s finding that their complaint did not meet that legal standard. In a statement, DOJ said it “disagrees with the Magistrate’s decision, which remarkably appears to suggest that high-ranking government officials are immune from accountability for making materially false statements to Congress.” “We are evaluating all options but cannot comment further on an ongoing criminal investigation. The Department’s actions will continue to be guided by the facts, the evidence, and the law — not politics,” the statement said. Faruqui previously criticized the government for attempting to bring additional charges against the ex-agents by filing a new unsigned complaint on the court docket without permission from a judge. Floris and Benavides had been targets of criticism from close allies of the president. Both had worked on security issues for the 2020 presidential election, which Trump has falsely claimed was stolen. In a statement, Floris’ attorneys said that while “Nikki should never have had to endure this disgraceful public attack, we hope the courts continue to be a refuge for all citizens unlawfully targeted by the Trump administration.” They said the charges against their client had been “nothing more than a politically-motivated smear campaign aimed at scoring political points before the midterm elections.” Attorneys for Benavides praised the judge’s decision, and called the accusations against their client “political theater.” “Bradley Benavides is a patriot,” the statement said. “He is a public servant. And he is innocent. We are grateful that Judge Faruqui carefully weighed the woefully inadequate evidence against the law, and found the government could not meet the extremely low burden of probable cause.” “We can only hope the government does not now go to the grand jury and try to charge this case behind closed doors, where they can shape the narrative and we are unable to present our side of the story,” it said.

articles.title: Trump administration brings California ballot fight to Supreme Court
articles.summary: The Trump administration on Monday brought its demand that California separate 20,000 mail ballots it says belong to likely noncitizens to the Supreme Court, thrusting the justices back into the center of the midterm campaign one day before Election Day. Lower courts have ruled the list isn’t credible and the Trump administration has no authority to…
articles.body:
The Trump administration on Monday brought its demand that California separate 20,000 mail ballots it says belong to likely noncitizens to the Supreme Court , thrusting the justices back into the center of the midterm campaign one day before Election Day.

Lower courts have ruled the list isn’t credible and the Trump administration has no authority to force the state to verify those voters’ citizenship, saying it would cause chaos if officials were to oblige.

“That doomsday prediction ignores that segregating ballots is a routine remedy when the lawfulness of ballots is questioned,” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote to the Supreme Court.

The fight over the 20,000 California ballots has rapidly escalated as Election Day approaches, as all sides agree they can’t be segregated once they’re processed. Hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been returned across the state, court filings show.

“If the United States is correct, and the individuals it has identified (or even some of those individuals) turn out to be aliens who are unlawfully voting in California, then the United States will suffer irreparable harm from the commingling of their ballots with lawful votes,” Sauer wrote.

Democrats and immigration groups have questioned the list’s veracity and warned the lawsuit is laying the groundwork to disenfranchise voters.

California says it’s not feasible to verify voters’ citizenship so late in the election cycle, and the state criticized the administration for refusing to say who supplied the list.

Lower courts have sided with the state as the Trump administration has raced for a judicial intervention . As it continues appealing, the administration has also sent subpoenas to local election officials and announced criminal charges against alleged noncitizens who’ve tried to register to vote.

The battle reached the Supreme Court after the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit sided against the administration in a 2-1 vote on Friday, saying segregating the ballots would have “potentially catastrophic effects on the entire system.”

The Trump administration’s Supreme Court appeal heads to Justice Elena Kagan, who by default handles emergency matters arising from California. Kagan has not yet announced a deadline for California to respond. She could act on the request alone or refer it to the full court for a vote.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D) said he had “strong reason” to believe his office would win again.

“This latest move reeks of desperation and is another attempt to undermine our elections and trample on the rule of law,” Bonta said in a statement. “If the U.S. Supreme Court calls for a response, we will be ready to defend the fundamental right to vote and push back against this lawlessness.”

“My message to Californians is simple: Election Day is tomorrow, but don’t wait until then to vote. If you haven’t cast your ballot yet, make a plan to do so as soon as possible. We’ll keep handling the legal fight in court,” Bonta continued.

articles.body:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) says Democrats will consider “next steps” for Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) when Congress reconvenes next week, after the lawmaker endorsed former Rep. Mike Rogers (R) in the Michigan Senate race.

“Haley Stevens made a terrible decision, blindsided everyone and isolated herself from the House Democratic Caucus,” Jeffries told Politico on Monday. “We will have a discussion about appropriate next steps upon our return.”

Both the House and Senate will be back in session on Nov. 9, less than a week after Election Day.

Stevens on Sunday put her support behind Rogers to succeed retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.) over progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed. She also recently appeared with the Republican on the campaign trail.

El-Sayed narrowly clinched victory in the Democratic primary over Stevens earlier this year, and tensions have risen in recent days between the two. The lawmaker’s fiance, who is Jewish, endorsed Rogers after voicing opposition to the progressive candidate’s stance on Israel.

House Democratic Caucus rules state that “in order to maintain membership in good standing, Members shall not participate in campaign activities for any candidate in a partisan federal election who is not a Member of the Democratic Party.”

Democrats, including Jeffries, have pushed back on Stevens’s decision — which she later defended — as the party looks to take control of both chambers of Congress next year.

“Let’s be clear about one thing. Dr. Abdul El-Sayed will always put the American people first and fight hard to lower the high cost of living,” the House Democratic leader posted Sunday on the social platform X. “His election is critical to flipping control of the United States Senate.”

Last week, El-Sayed told Stevens to avoid his campaign events and disinvited her from a planned appearance , a source familiar with the matter told NewsNation, The Hill’s sister network. He also fired back at her after the lawmaker expected him to apologize about previous comments seen as antisemitic.

“So, while Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, let’s all focus on the task at hand: that’s beating Mike Rogers, holding Trump accountable, and getting money out of politics,” El-Sayed wrote Friday online.

Curtis Hertel, who chairs the Michigan Democratic Party, said Sunday in a post on X that “Congresswoman Stevens is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future.”

The Hill has reached out to the lawmaker’s office for comment.

articles.title: Will tomorrow’s elections even matter?
articles.summary: For Donald Trump, no matter how the election is decided, he stands to gain.
articles.body:
Tomorrow, Americans will go to the polls to choose their local, state and federal elected officials. While every race is important to some group, intense focus will be on the congressional elections.

Regardless of how long it takes to tally the votes, these outcomes will determine the future composition of the 120th Congress: Either Democrats or Republicans will win control of both chambers, or Congress will be divided, presumably with Democrats having the House and Republicans the Senate.

No matter the final result, will the federal government be able to govern and resolve voters’ most critical issues ?

Affordability — both the economy and the cost of living — and corruption intensified by growing chasms between the rich and everyone else, were the two most dominant, according to Bloomberg, followed by the war in Iran. Costs of virtually everything from airline tickets to healthcare to Zyrtec, an anti-allergy pill, have soared. This has created great economic anxiety.

Yet, despite the rhetoric and campaigns that in some cases had no “ bottom ” to the vulgarity and ferocious coarseness expressed, what plans do Democrats and Republicans have in place to respond to the voters? The answers are between few and none. And the big winner power-wise is the president, even if his name was not on any ballot.

For Donald Trump, no matter how the election is decided, he stands to gain. If the Republicans hold both Houses, Congress will remain a rubber stamp and doormat, fearful of challenging or even questioning a lame duck leader because he almost certainly will determine his successor as candidate for the Oval Office.

Should the Democrats sweep both chambers, or just the House, it is clear on whom Trump will vent his anger and blame. Executive orders will become even more plentiful and the de facto means of governing. When or if the courts intervene, as in the past, Trump will merely find another law or argument to justify a replacement executive order.

While a Democratic House may launch investigations, a third impeachment of the president is unlikely to be on the agenda, unless the Dems win the Senate or can count on 67 votes in the Senate to convict. Despite the possible grounds for an indictment, lesser members of the administration, in particular the Defense secretary, will be targeted.

But will a slew of investigations provide any better solutions to the nation’s ills, and the voters worries and fears? Probably not.

How, for example, will the affordability issue be broached? The high costs of energy and diesel fuel as well as fertilizer, for example, are entirely due to the war with Iran and the cut-off of oil and nitrates from the Persian Gulf. Only the president can end the war, unless the Democrats won control of both Houses or had enough votes in the Senate to invoke the War Powers Act . But would the president listen and follow the law, as he could veto any legislation?

Congress could override the veto, although the two-thirds majority needed seems unlikely. In that case, Congress could cut off funding, as it did to put a final nail in the Vietnam coffin. Still, as the president has shifted funds in the budget for other purposes, could he not do the same again?

On corruption, legislation to elevate or set ethical and moral standards is a mission impossible. Trump can assert that his assets are in a trust over which he has no control. And his globetrotting, deal making sons and son-in-law are private citizens. Surely no law could or should prevent them from making a living.

As for the gap between rich and poor and the influence of money in politics, the Supreme Court’s Citizens v. United gave money the constitutional protection of free speech. That made Elon Musk the second most powerful man in America, contributing nearly half a billion dollars — a mere pittance to a trillionaire — to help buy congressional seats. And ironically, Musk is the only person who can end the Russia-Ukraine War by cutting off Kyiv’s access to his Starlink and Starshield military technology.

What does this mean? Democrats and a number of independents believe that with his policies on tariffs, immigration enforcement, tax cuts for the rich and provoking wars that need not be fought, Trump has wrecked this country in less than two years. However, without clear cut legislation that can be passed and sustained over a veto, Democrats will be forced to wait until at least 2028.

But can the nation afford to wait that long?

Harlan Ullman is chairman of a private company and principal author of the doctrine of shock and awe. His next book, co-written with Field Marshal The Lord David Richards, former United Kingdom chief of defense and due out this Fall, is “Who Thinks Best Wins: How Decisive Strategic Thinking Will Prevent Global Chaos.”

articles.title: Talarico campaigns alongside Democrat who called ICE 'new KKK' and demanded its abolition
articles.summary: James Talarico praised Frederick Haynes III at a Texas rally, a congressional candidate who compared ICE to the KKK and called to abolish it.
articles.body: James Talarico, a U.S. Senate candidate in Texas, briefly praised Frederick Haynes III, a Democratic congressional candidate who compared President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement efforts to the KKK, at a get-out-the-vote event on Thursday as part of his Clear Eyes Full Hearts tour. "Give it up for your next congressman, Dr. Freddy Haynes. Thank you, Dr. Haynes, for those kind words and for your service to this community," Talarico said, following an introduction and speech from Haynes. Although Talarico has not issued a formal endorsement of Haynes, the moment is notable for Talarico as he pitches himself as a Democrat who can represent the values of the Republican-leaning Lone Star State — and as he tries to distance himself from controversy over past remarks Republicans have characterized as woke. TALARICO RALLY WARMUP ACT CALLS FOR ABOLISHING ICE, CONTRASTING SENATE HOPEFUL'S MESSAGE Haynes, the pastor of Friendship-West Baptist Church, has framed many of his political views in the context of race and did so again on the event with Talarico. "You transformed ICE into the new KKK and brought about terror in this nation," Haynes said of Trump's use of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). "It’s time to melt ICE. It’s time to abolish ICE," Haynes added. Haynes is running to fill the seat of Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, the incumbent in Texas' 30th Congressional District who gave up her seat in a Senate bid she ultimately lost. During his campaign, Haynes has framed his support for climate policy as a fight against "environmental racism." He has also accused conservatives and the Trump administration of benefiting from fears of Black advancement. "They have used Black people and perceived Black progress as the boogeyman. We have not witnessed this kind of corruption, this kind of blatant corruption," Haynes said in an October interview. "We are witnessing the demolishing of what democratic infrastructure was built by the gains of the civil rights movement," Haynes added. Even before his congressional run, Haynes made political commentary that relied heavily on a racial lens. After the death of Charlie Kirk, a conservative political commentator who started Turning Point USA, Haynes described Kirk as a man with views "rooted in White supremacy" and contrasted it with the deaths of Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X. "A White Christian gets killed, murdered — not assassinated. We going to tell the whole truth today. Martin King got assassinated. Malcolm X got assassinated. Medgar Evers got assassinated. Don’t compare Kirk to King," Haynes said in a September 2025 address to his church. UN PUSHES NATIONS TO CONSIDER SLAVERY REPARATIONS BUT LEGAL GROUP SAYS IDEA 'NOT GOING TO FLY IN THE US' Haynes would go on to condemn Kirk's death and political violence. Haynes has also said he was a personal supporter of reparations. "America, you owe us. What you done to us has been immoral. It’s been evil. It’s been unjust. It’s been downright wrong and the only way to bring salvation to America — you gotta pay us what you owe us," Haynes said at a Solidarity for Reparations event at a San Francisco church. "I've come by to say, San Francisco, California, Texas, United States of America, if you want salvation to come to this house, you've got to engage in reparations." For his own part, Talarico has also supported the idea of reparations, framing it as an outflow of his religious convictions. "Reparations, repairing past harms, is part of my faith tradition. It’s part of the values I was raised with," Talarico said in a town hall meeting in July. "We have to correct the injustices of our past." In the closing days of his campaign, Talarico has argued that, despite some of his views on race and gender which run counter to conservative stances, he could still represent Texas as a moderate. TALARICO SAYS HE 'MISSED THE MARK' AS HE BACKTRACKS ON CONTROVERSIAL WOKE STATEMENTS "Our campaign has been able to show that you can be a more moderate, reasonable candidate and still be exciting," Talarico said in October. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Talarico’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment if his comment about Haynes should be viewed as an endorsement of his platform or his views on race in politics.

articles.body:
It’s Monday. A lingering candy hangover from Halloween combined with the anticipation for Election Day tomorrow has made for quite the stew so far today. Shall we?

Programming note : Hello! We are Steff Danielle Thomas and Elliott Davis filling in for Cate. Please send your tips, comments and story ideas to sthomas@thehill.com or edavis@thehill.com .

Know a lobbyist who moved the needle this year? Nominate them for The Hill’s 2026 Top Lobbyists by Friday, Nov. 6 . Submit through this form only:

The Associated Press | Charlie Neibergall

President Trump this afternoon is set to give remarks at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool — a final push to sell Americans on his agenda before voters go to the polls Tuesday and determine how much of a counterweight his administration will face in Congress for the remainder of his second term.

Choosing the landmark as the site of his speech is emblematic of the Trump administration’s efforts toward remaking Washington, in Trump’s vision, from the White House’s East Wing to the Kennedy Center. (Two-thirds of respondents to a July Washington Post/Ipsos survey disapproved of Trump’s White House ballroom, reflecting pool Reflecting Pool and triumphal arch projects, specifically.)

The president, nonetheless, is expected to promote the beautification projects on Monday afternoon, and he told reporters on Sunday that making his remarks at the reflecting pool will “show how beautiful it is.”

Need a reminder of what else Trump has sought to give a facelift in Washington? The Hill’s Sarah Davis and Finya Swai recently wrote a rundown .

The speech will also act as Trump’s pre-midterms closing message, focusing on the agenda he and Republican lawmakers have advanced since he returned to the Oval Office last year, a source familiar told The Hill’s broadcast partner NewsNation.

It might be a tough sell: A new poll from NBC News found that 60 percent of those surveyed disapproved of Trump’s job performance , and a majority of Republican respondents were dissatisfied with the state of the economy. The Hill’s election partner Decision Desk HQ estimated Monday that Democrats have an 84 percent chance of winning the House and a 65 percent chance of taking control of the Senate.

Shockwaves are still spreading after Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) endorsed her state’s Republican Senate nominee, former Rep. Mike Rogers , instead of fellow Democrat Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday.

The endorsement, which came after El-Sayed disinvited Stevens from what was supposed to be their first joint appearance in a show of Democratic unity before Election Day, prompted a number of resignations from Stevens’s staff and even rare praise of a Democrat from Trump.

Need to get caught up on yesterday’s bombshell? The Hill’s Caroline Vakil and Amie Parnes covered Democrats’ sharp criticism of Stevens’s move. Caroline also wrote about El-Sayed’s response .

But the Democratic Senate nominee might not be sweating too much: El-Sayed’s campaign raised $1.2 million in just four hours after Stevens endorsed Rogers. The number marked El-Sayed’s second-best single-day fundraising total since he won the nomination, The Hill confirmed.

There was certainly no shortage of news on Sunday: A federal judge dismissed the Justice Department’s lawsuit that seeks to block certification of the Alaska Senate race results if Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) loses his reelection bid.

It marks a loss for the Trump administration ahead of Election Day, when Alaska’s Democratic nominee, former Rep. Mary Peltola , will appear on the Last Frontier’s ballot alongside the GOP incumbent and similarly named Dan Sullivan .

Peltola has denied any knowledge of her campaign’s alleged recruitment of the other Sullivan, which federal officials are investigating .

The accused “ballot stacking” scheme was first reported by The New York Times.

The president is already planning his next act if Democrats take control of Congress next year: Meet “Mr. Veto.”

In an interview with the New York Post’s Miranda Devine set to air Monday, Trump said he would embrace the nickname if Republicans lost their majorities.

“I’m not going to let them through,” he said, adding that repeated vetoes could eventually bring both parties to the negotiating table.

The odds : The comments come as election forecasters increasingly see a path for Democrats to take the lead both chambers of Congress, potentially turning Trump into a lame-duck president for the final two years of his term.

He has been here before : the GOP lost control of the House during his first term, setting up battles over border security and presidential war powers. And if history is any indication, his veto pen could get quite the workout.

Emails from the Social Security Administration and IRS praising the president are raising legal eyebrows .

Experts say the messages, sent just days before the midterms, could violate the Hatch Act, which restricts political activity by federal employees.

The emails, according to the Times , touted his leadership and tax cuts, prompting questions about whether government resources were being used for political promotion.

The Hill’s Decision Desk ’26: Election Night In America will be moderated by Cory Smith and Drew Petrimoulx , joined by Chris Stirewalt and other special guests. The live special features sharp analysis on the most consequential races across the country, the biggest developments in real time, and live race calls powered by election data provider Decision Desk HQ . Watch us on your preferred streaming platform or on TheHill.com.

articles.title: Kansas Senate race: Will faith decide who wins the heartland?
articles.summary: Kansas cattle ranchers and farmers say they are politically divided.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Will faith make the difference for voters in Kansas who are torn between the Republican and Democratic candidates?

The unexpectedly tight midterms race for Kansas' Senate seat between Republican Sen. Roger Marshall and his Democratic opponent, Rev. Adam Hamilton , suggests the answer is yes — so much so that it could help decide control of the Senate.

Hamilton is a pastor, and he campaigns like one. He prays over voters, invokes the Bible with ease and counters attack ads calling him "woke" with quips like: "If Jesus were here, you would call him too woke."

He has put a notable distance between himself and Democrats on the coasts: He told POLITICO that Chuck Schumer is a "liability" in Kansas and that Kamala Harris should stay in California.

Ahead of Tuesday's Senate election, Kansas cattle ranchers and farmers interviewed by NewsNation all expressed concerns about rising costs, but they're divided politically. One longtime Republican-leaning farmer who voted for President Donald Trump in 2016 says he's now inclined to vote for Hamilton over Marshall.

Kansas hasn't elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century. The latest Decision Desk HQ polling shows Hamilton leading Marshall 48.7%-45.3%.

articles.title: Abortion, transgender rights and voter ID: These are the major 2026 midterms ballot measures voters will decide tomorrow
articles.summary: Ballot measures voters a way to directly alter their state laws, rather than relying solely on legislators to create policy on their behalf.
articles.body:
The battle for control of Congress is getting the lion's share of the attention in the lead-up to the midterms, but there are a lot of other consequential measures that'll appear on ballots tomorrow that could have a direct impact on voters' lives.

Ballot measures often don't receive much national attention, but every two years, voters across the country decide whether to adopt policies that have major implications for their states. This year is no different.

There are more than 140 total measures collectively across 40 states this year. Many touch on some of the biggest issues in U.S. politics, including abortion, transgender rights, voting and the democratic process itself.

Ballot measures can give the people a way to directly alter the laws in their states instead of relying solely on their elected representatives to create policy on their behalf. In some cases, they provide an opportunity for voters to endorse or reject something their state legislature wants to do. In other cases, regular citizens can get their preferred policy on the ballot directly through a signature-gathering campaign.

Here's a rundown of some of the major measures on statewide ballots this year.

The Supreme Court's 2022 decision to overturn the nationwide abortion protections established by Roe v. Wade instantly turned abortion access into a state-by-state issue. It also led to a flurry of ballot measures across the country in which voters were asked to decide whether their states should protect or restrict abortion rights. In the years since, voters have generally come down in favor of protecting abortion rights.

That trend will get another test this year due to abortion-related measures in four states.

In Idaho , voters will decide whether to overturn their state's strict abortion restrictions and establish a right to reproductive freedom and privacy, including abortion until fetal viability. If the measure passes, Idaho will become the latest red state where voters have used a ballot initiative to expand abortion rights.

One of those red states is Missouri , where voters approved a measure in 2024 that struck down some of the nation's most restrictive abortion laws. A Republican-backed measure on this year's ballot would repeal that 2024 amendment and allow strict abortion restrictions to be put back into place. The same measure would also create new limits on gender-affirming care in the state.

Two other states that already have relatively permissive laws around abortion access — Nevada and Virginia — are voting on measures that would enshrine abortion rights in their state constitutions, a step that would make it much harder to restrict access in the future.

The debate over transgender rights, particularly when it comes to minors, has become a central issue in American politics. It should be no surprise, then, that a number of states have measures related to the topic on the ballot this year. All of them would impose new limits on transgender rights.

Four states — Washington , Nebraska , Arizona and Colorado — will vote on measures that would ban trans athletes from participating on sports teams that match their gender identity. There are some important differences from state to state, though. The proposals in Washington and Nebraska would only apply to girls' and women's teams. Colorado's and Arizona's would apply to both male and female teams.

Washington's bill also includes a stipulation that would require all K-12 students, whether they identify as trans or not, who want to play girls' or women's sports to have their sex verified by a doctor . Arizona's measure would also ban schools from allowing trans minors or adults to access bathrooms, locker rooms or other private spaces designated for a sex that doesn't match the one they were assigned at birth.

A separate initiative in Colorado would ban gender-affirming surgeries for minors. Missouri's measure would go even further. In addition to banning the surgeries, it would also prohibit minors from receiving other forms of gender-affirming care, like hormone therapy and puberty blockers.

Six states will vote on measures related to voter ID.

Those in California, Colorado and Nevada would either establish or expand laws requiring voters to show ID when they cast their ballots. Each of the proposals would also require voter ID for mail-in ballots.

Arizona, Ohio and North Carolina already have strict voter ID requirements in place under state law, but measures in each state would add or expand those requirements in their state constitutions.

Schools have been a major flash point for culture war battles in recent years. A handful of measures on the ballot in November will ask voters to weigh in on some of those debates.

Arizona and Wisconsin both have measures that would ban affirmative action in schools and all other government agencies.

Alabama has a pair of proposals. One would require public schools to play the national anthem at least once a week. The other would make the recitation of the Pledge of Allegiance a daily requirement and mandate school boards to adopt policies that allow student-led prayer.

A sweeping parental rights initiative in Washington would give parents of public school students substantially more oversight over the education their children receive, including the power to review curricula and textbooks. It would also put strict new limits on the kinds of medical care schools can provide without parental notification and roll back changes to the state's parental rights law that protected against discrimination and bullying in schools.

Ballot measures frequently center on contentious political issues, but in recent years, the initiative process itself has increasingly become the subject of political debate.

Five states will vote on measures that would make it harder for citizen-led ballot initiatives to become law. They would accomplish that by either raising the share of the vote certain measures need to get approved or restricting the subjects that initiatives can address.

Voters in California and Utah will consider measures that would require certain initiatives that would raise taxes to receive more than the simple majority of support they currently need to be successful. California's would raise the bar for voter-proposed local special taxes to two-thirds of the vote. Utah's would set the new standard for tax-related citizen initiatives at 60%. North Dakota and South Dakota both have measures that would require any attempt to change their state constitutions to get 60% of the vote.

Changing the threshold for success by 10 percentage points may not sound like a huge deal, but it is often the difference between a proposal becoming law and being rejected. For example, initiatives in Florida that would have legalized abortion and recreational marijuana use both received majority support from voters in 2024, but neither became law because they fell short of the state's 60% approval standard.

Idaho has a measure on the ballot that would ban initiatives aimed at legalizing marijuana, psychedelics and other narcotics. If it passes, only the state legislature would have the power to legalize or decriminalize those substances.

Another two states will decide on measures designed to protect the initiative process. A proposal in Montana would amend the state's constitution to guarantee citizens' rights to pursue ballot initiatives and make it harder for the government to interfere with measures approved by voters.

In Missouri , voters will weigh in on a measure that would prohibit the state's Republican-led legislature from weakening the initiative process. It would also bar it from amending or repealing any measures that have passed unless 80% of both chambers agree to put the change before voters.

There are many pivotal ballot initiatives being considered across the country that don't fit neatly into a specific category. Here are a few of them.

Alaska voters will decide whether to repeal their state's recently adopted ranked-choice voting system. A proposal in Arizona would ban new traffic cameras without direct voter approval. Nebraska will choose whether to legalize online sports betting . Vermont will consider a measure that would ban discrimination based on gender identity. Virginia will decide if people convicted of felonies should have their right to vote restored once they're released from prison. A measure in Wisconsin would prohibit the government from closing places of worship during public health emergencies. Massachusetts will consider whether recreational marijuana sales should once again be made illegal. A proposal on the ballot in North Dakota would require all public schools to provide free breakfast and lunch.

Lower-stakes — but still noteworthy — measures under consideration include a Colorado initiative that would enshrine the right to hunt and fish in the state constitution and a request for Idaho voters to select an official state gun .

articles.title: Stevens ‘flushed herself down the toilet’: Van Jones
articles.summary: Liberal commentator Van Jones on Sunday described Rep. Haley Stevens’s (R-Mich.) recent endorsement of GOP Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers as flushing “herself down the toilet.” During a panel on CNN on Sunday night, Jones praised Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s message discipline in the wake of Stevens’s endorsement of Rogers. “You know, Abdul,…
articles.body:
Liberal commentator Van Jones on Sunday described Rep. Haley Stevens’s (R-Mich.) recent endorsement of GOP Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers as flushing “herself down the toilet.”

During a panel on CNN on Sunday night, Jones praised Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s message discipline in the wake of Stevens’s endorsement of Rogers.

“You know, Abdul, when given the opportunity to follow this whole conversation down a rabbit hole, had incredible message discipline today, and kept talking about Michigan voters. When Haley was talking about Michigan voters, she had moral authority. She starts talking about herself, she loses moral authority,” Jones said on “Anderson Cooper 360.”

“He could have done the same thing and gotten personal. He didn’t. Abdul said, ‘I don’t want to talk about this woman at all. I want to talk about people 15 minutes from here.’ Now listen, I think his message has been too narrow, and he’s left out too many people. But he has shown a level of discipline on this campaign, and Haley just flushed herself down the toilet,” Jones added.

On Sunday, El-Sayed brushed off Stevens’s endorsement of Rogers, stating it didn’t carry weight and that he was focused on Michigan’s issues.

“At the end of the day, I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens,” El-Sayed told reporters Sunday in Detroit.

“This is a state of 10 million people who deserve a lot better from the government. I’m a lot more focused on the 9,999,998 that are not the ones you guys are talking about,” he said.

Stevens on Sunday endorsed Rogers to serve in the Senate over El-Sayed, who defeated Stevens in a tense primary battle this summer. Her announcement followed days of feuding between herself and El-Sayed and came just two days before the midterm elections.

Stevens said she would appear last weekend alongside El-Sayed for the first time since their primary earlier this year, but she went after him for his response to a controversial anti-Israel ad that seemed to connect the country to high grocery prices in the U.S.

El-Sayed then told Stevens to avoid his campaign events and disinvited her from a planned appearance on Sunday, a source familiar with the matter told NewsNation, The Hill’s sister network. El-Sayed also fired back at Stevens after she expected him to apologize due to his remarks on Israel.

The Hill has reached out to Stevens’s office for comment.
