articles.title: Don’t kill license plate readers: Instead, have Congress rewrite the rules
articles.summary: Former police chief Brian O’Hara argues that instead of banning license plate readers due to privacy concerns and misuse, Congress should implement strict federal regulations regarding data retention, independent oversight, and manual verification.
articles.body:
Last September, weeks after a gunman opened fire on children at Annunciation Catholic Church , another man threatened to shoot up another Minneapolis school. Our officers used license plate readers to follow his car out of the state . With help from a sheriff’s office near Kansas City , he was in custody in Missouri within three hours.

That is this technology on its best day. On its worst, it lets an officer track a former partner’s car dozens of times , or hands federal agents a map of where a city’s residents drive . Both are true. Washington is answering the second by throwing away the first.

A growing list of cities have dropped Flock Safety, the industry’s largest vendor. The bipartisan “Flock-Off Act” would cut federal funds to any department that keeps them. The Ban Flock Act from Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) would do the same from the left. When a Senate Judiciary subcommittee invited the vendors’ CEOs to testify last month, none showed up . The loudest voice on the other side is President Trump, whose defense is, “I like them.”

I understand the anger. I led the Minneapolis Police Department after George Floyd’s murder, and the Newark Police Department before that. It takes only one officer trampling civil liberties to destroy trust earned by thousands. Critics are right about the abuses. Dozens of officers have been fired or charged for using plate readers to stalk people.

But the backlash is aimed at the wrong target. The problem was never the camera; it is the absence of governance. Only one bill, Sen. Josh Hawley’s (R-Mo.) Stop Flock Abuse Act , tries to write rules to provide that, and even that leaves the most important job to the agencies themselves.

The tradeoff is real. Atlantic City put readers on every road in and out of town, and a peer-reviewed study found shootings, car thefts and property crime all fell. Austin dropped Flock in 2025. After a shooting spree this spring, its Democratic mayor said the cameras “would have been helpful.”

Three rules matter most; nearly every bill gets at least two wrong.

First, retention. New Jersey keeps plate data for three years ; even Flock now defaults to a week . But a bill moving in Trenton would delete nearly everything within 48 hours . That does not protect privacy. It destroys evidence and punishes victims. A witness isn’t immediately located; a victim knocked out regains consciousness days later; a family on vacation returns to a home burglarized. In any of these scenarios, under a 48-hour rule — critical evidence is gone. NYU Law’s Policing Project has a better answer. Police purge after about a week, and a sealed copy sits with the state attorney general for a year — off limits without a warrant. Keep the evidence, lock it away, give the key to a judge.

Second, oversight. Every bill is weak on protecting civil liberties; the solution they proposed is for agencies to audit themselves. New Jersey’s last statewide audit , run by the State Police, itself a major user, covered 517 agencies and found two significant violations. Illinois agencies never caught federal immigration agents in their camera data. The Secretary of State’s auditors did, and it was against state law. Minneapolis went through an independent audit while I was chief. We passed, and we still came out with tighter rules. That is the point of an outsider — they see what you cannot, and when they clear you, the public has reason to accept it.

Third, verification. Cameras misread plates, hot lists go stale; yet almost no bill addresses it. In Aurora, Colo., officers acting on a false hit forced a woman and four girls to lie face-down in a parking lot at gunpoint . It cost the city $1.9 million. The Senate’s own witness last month was a Florida woman jailed after a camera misidentified her SUV as the vehicle fleeing a fatal crash. Those were not camera failures. They were failures to check. No one should be stopped until an officer confirms the alert is accurate and current.

Tear the cameras down instead, and two things happen. Many of the towns that “dropped” Flock have already signed with a competitor ; the cameras are not going anywhere. And the next shooting spree will bring back the rest, the same way they arrived the first time: with no rules at all.

The danger was never the camera on the pole. It is the database behind it, and who gets to open it. In Newark and Minneapolis, reform meant guardrails set by someone other than the police, and consequences for crossing them. The backlash has handed Congress something it rarely gets on policing — public attention and bipartisan agreement that something has to change. Write the rules and keep the tool; the public needs both.

Brian O’Hara served as deputy mayor and public safety director in Newark, N.J., and as the 54th chief of the Minneapolis Police Department. He is a Distinguished Fellow at the Rutgers Center on Public Security and principal of the O’Hara Leadership Group .

articles.title: Judge dismisses charges against FBI agents involved in Hunter Biden case
articles.summary: A federal judge tossed charges accusing two former FBI officials of lying to Congress about Hunter Biden investigation.
articles.body:
A federal judge has dismissed a criminal case against two former senior FBI officials accused of lying to Congress about former President Joe Biden’s son, Hunter.

On Monday, US Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui ruled that prosecutors, under the direction of the Department of Justice, lacked sufficient evidence to move the case forward and expressed concern that the investigation was rushed, overtly political and dogged by “critical mistakes”.

He said it “cannot be described as anything other than weaponization”.

“I will not bury my head in the sand and pretend I cannot read a calendar,” Faruqui said in court, referring to its proximity to the midterms. “I will not lobotomize myself that way.”

The case suggested that Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides misled Congress in 2023 by lying about their knowledge of and involvement in an investigation into a laptop the Justice Department said was dropped off at a Delaware tech shop in 2019 by Hunter Biden.

An FBI agent who worked on the case testified that the investigation into Floris and Benavides began last July under the direction of FBI Director Kash Patel. The Associated Press news agency reported that the case echoed complaints by President Donald Trump and his allies that potentially damaging information about the Biden family was suppressed during the 2020 election, which Trump lost.

The Justice Department may still have the chance to pursue a grand jury indictment of the former FBI officials.

Nonetheless, Faruqui’s early ruling and concerns about the case hamper the Justice Department’s case.

In a preliminary hearing last week, the judge pointed out that the Justice Department was not acting in accordance with legal procedure when it filed an amended complaint with an additional charge without first clearing the charge with the court — something he said he had never seen before.

articles.title: Will Republicans or Democrats win control of the Senate in the 2026 midterms? These are key races to watch tomorrow.
articles.summary: The GOP's majority is on the line as Democrats look to flip seats in a handful of historically red states.
articles.body:
Control of both chambers of Congress is up for grabs tomorrow. But as important as the House of Representatives is, all signs point to the true drama of the midterms being in the battle for the Senate.

There are 35 Senate seats on the ballot this year. Most of those races won't be competitive. The balance of power in the Senate will be decided by the dozen or so states where the outcome truly is uncertain. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority, which means they can lose three seats and still maintain control of the chamber — thanks to Vice President JD Vance's constitutionally granted power to break ties in an evenly split Senate.

Forecasters widely expect Democrats to flip the House, but view the Senate as a "true toss-up."

The key Senate battlegrounds include traditional swing states, idiosyncratic areas of the Northeast and historically Republican states where Democrats have rarely been competitive in recent elections.

The outcome will have enormous implications for the final two years of President Trump's tenure in the White House. Democrats only need to gain control of one chamber to have the power to block or reshape Trump's legislative agenda. But a Senate majority would empower them to do much more. They would have an effective veto over Trump's nominees for high-ranking Cabinet positions and could block him from appointing any new Supreme Court justices. Control over key Senate committees would also allow Democrats to launch sweeping investigations into Trump and his administration.

Here's a rundown of the races that will likely decide which party controls the Senate after the midterms.

True to the state's image, there's a wildness to Alaska's Senate race that you won't find elsewhere in the country. On paper, incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan should be well-positioned to win a third term in the Senate. Alaska is a consistently red state that has only elected a Democrat to the Senate once in the past 45 years. Democrats' challenges in the state have been so acute recently that they didn't even have a candidate on the ballot the last time Sullivan was up for reelection.

But forecasters expect this year's race to be much closer. Sullivan's main opponent is former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola , who was Alaska's lone member of the House from 2022 to 2025. Peltola, the first Alaska Native and first woman to represent the Last Frontier in Congress, is a rare Democrat with a record of success in statewide elections.

The race suddenly received a surge in national attention after the Department of Justice filed a lawsuit on Oct. 22 to block certification of the election if Sen. Sullivan suffers a close loss, alleging that retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan is a Democratic plant whose purpose is to confuse voters and siphon away votes. The New York Times later reported that operatives aligned with Peltola helped recruit the second Sullivan to run. Peltola denied any involvement in the alleged plot. The lawsuit was dismissed by a federal judge in Alaska on Sunday; however, the DOJ said it plans to appeal that decision. Some congressional Republicans have also suggested that Peltola should not be allowed to be seated in the Senate if she wins.

It would likely take a major blue wave election for incumbent Republican Sen. Ashley Moody to be at a real risk of being unseated by progressive Democrat Angie Nixon. The GOP has won the last two Senate races in Florida by an average of 14 points. Polls have shown Nixon trailing by a smaller margin than that, but still far enough behind for forecasters to rate the race as favoring Republicans.

On top of flipping a handful of GOP-held seats, Democrats' chances of gaining control of the Senate rely on keeping the ones they already have. One of the most important is in Georgia.

Sen. Jon Ossoff became a rising star within the Democratic Party when he pulled off a stunning upset in the 2020 elections, defeating incumbent Republican David Perdue in an extremely tight runoff. Ossoff is now running for reelection for the first time. His opponent is Rep. Mike Collins, a MAGA-friendly congressman who has created controversy with a series of divisive social media posts during his tenure in the House.

More recently, Collins has faced intense scrutiny over his social media posts and the online activity of people close to him , including his son-in-law .

Polls have shown Ossoff with a healthy lead over Collins, enough of a gap that forecasters at the non-partisan Center for Politics wrote in July that it would be a "true shock" if he isn't reelected.

It wasn't that long ago that Iowa was viewed as one of the country's quintessential swing states, but the Hawkeye State has shifted significantly to the right over the past decade — to the point where it's no longer competitive in presidential elections.

That said, polls suggest Democrats appear to have a real chance of flipping the Senate seat held by retiring incumbent Joni Ernst. Their nominee is Josh Turek, a state lawmaker and two-time Paralympic gold medalist. A moderate who describes himself as a "prairie populist," Turek has focused heavily on how Trump's tariffs and the war with Iran have affected farmers in his state throughout the campaign.

His opponent is GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson, a former local news anchor who cruised to the Republican nomination after earning Trump's endorsement. Polling of the race has fluctuated significantly, with both candidates showing small leads at different times.

It has been almost 100 years since Kansas elected a Democrat to the Senate, but the state may be in play this year as incumbent Republican Roger Marshall looks to keep the GOP's nearly century-long winning streak alive.

His opponent is Adam Hamilton, a pastor and the founder of the nation's largest United Methodist church. Polls in the final weeks of the campaign have mostly shown Hamilton ahead. Libertarian Party candidate David Graham is also on the ballot and has drawn a small but potentially significant share of support in some polls.

Democrats have been eyeing Sen. Susan Collins's seat for decades, but the Republican has fended off every challenger they've sent her way during her 30 years in the Senate. Her opponent this time around will be Troy Jackson , a former logger and longtime member of the state legislature. Jackson was chosen at a hastily planned convention after the party's original nominee, Graham Platner, dropped out of the race following an allegation of sexual assault, which he denied, among other controversies.

Collins has historically managed to outperform other Republicans when she's been on the ballot, even in "blue wave" years like 2020, in part because of her longstanding reputation as a relative moderate within her party. But that image is being tested in this race. Jackson has centered much of his campaign on tying Collins to some of the more high-profile times she's sided with the president on major issues, particularly her votes to confirm Supreme Court justices who later joined the majority in overturning Roe v. Wade .

Jackson faces his own challenges. He has been playing catch-up after becoming the nominee so late in the process. He will also face scrutiny over his past conservative positions on issues like abortion and same-sex marriage, which are a far cry from the progressive political views he expresses today.

One of the nation's few genuine swing states is home to one of the most pivotal midterm matchups. Incumbent Democrat Gary Peters opted not to run for a third term, setting the stage for a nailbiter of a Democratic primary in which progressive physician Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeated Rep. Haley Stevens, a relative moderate, in a major victory for the party's left wing. There was far less drama on the Republican side, where former Rep. Mike Rogers cruised to the GOP nomination.

Rogers was also the Republican nominee in 2024, losing to Democrat Elissa Slotkin by 0.34 percentage points of the vote in one of the tightest Senate races in the country. El-Sayed, who supports policies like a billionaire's tax and Medicare for All, will need the support of centrist Democrats and swing voters in order to build a big enough coalition to win. Polls have shown El-Sayed in front late in the race, but with margins small enough to make a win by Rogers entirely plausible. It's unclear how a surprise endorsement from El-Sayed's Democratic primary opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens, might shift the race in its final stages.

Incumbent Sen. Tina Smith has opted not to run for a second term, which could help create an opening for Republicans to break Democrats' longstanding hold on Minnesota's U.S. Senate delegation.

To pursue that goal, the GOP has enlisted a rare political newcomer with widespread name recognition: Former sports broadcaster Michele Tafoya. Her Democratic opponent is Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan.

The race so far has been defined by the remarkably different approaches of the two candidates. Tafoya has worked to push her party toward the political center, portraying herself as a moderate Republican and mostly focusing on issues like affordability and public safety while steering clear of some of the more divisive parts of Trump's agenda. Flanagan, on the other hand, is a progressive who represents a significant step to the left on policy for Democrats relative to Smith.

Polls have shown Flanagan leading by a few points in the late stages of the race.

In a state as red as Nebraska, rather than fielding their own candidate to challenge incumbent Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts, Democrats have thrown their support behind independent candidate Dan Osborn.

This is the second time that Osborn, a Navy veteran and former labor union leader, has run for the Senate in a race without a Democratic candidate. Two years ago, he finished about 6 points behind GOP Sen. Deb Fisher in the state's closest Senate race in more than two decades.

Osborn has been deeply critical of both parties and says he opposes parts of the Democratic Party's platform. But if he's elected, the GOP would lose a Senate seat it currently holds and one vote that it can comfortably count on in support of Trump's legislative agenda.

The Granite State is rarely discussed as a swing state because it consistently votes for Democrats in presidential elections. But Senate races are a different story. Several Republicans have been elected to represent New Hampshire in the Senate in recent decades. One of them is John Sununu, who is running to regain the seat he lost in 2008 when he was defeated by Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, the retiring incumbent. Sununu is part of a political dynasty in the state. His father, also named John, and his brother Chris both served as governor.

The Democratic nominee is Rep. Chris Pappas, a moderate who comfortably outpaced a democratic socialist rival in his party's primary. Pappas is the first gay man to represent New Hampshire in Congress and would become the first openly gay male senator in U.S. history if he is elected.

If polls are accurate, Republicans have a lot of ground to make up if they want to hold on to this seat from the Tarheel State. Incumbent Sen. Thom Tillis, a rare member of the GOP caucus to defy the president in some circumstances, has opted not to seek reelection. The Republican nominee to replace him is Michael Whatley, a former chair of the Republican National Committee.

Whatley has a strong history in North Carolina, having run the state Republican Party for nearly five years, but he lacks the statewide name recognition of his Democratic opponent, former Gov. Roy Cooper.

Both of Cooper's gubernatorial wins were reasonably close, but polls have shown him with a significant lead over Whatley. Forecasters have also shifted the race toward Democrats.

The Buckeye State has trended to the right over the past decade or so, but a unique set of circumstances has contributed to making this race a genuine toss-up in the eyes of some forecasters. Aside from the Democratic and Republican nominees, Libertarian William Redpath and Greg Levy of the Party for Socialism and Liberation are also on the ballot. These two lesser-known candidates are getting as much as 6% of voters' support in polls, collectively, which is potentially enough to influence the outcome in a very tight race.

Husted is the rare incumbent with less experience than his challenger. He has only been in the Senate since 2025, when he was appointed to fill the vacancy created when JD Vance became vice president. Brown, on the other hand, served three full terms in the Senate before losing his seat to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024. Brown also has a massive cash advantage, which has allowed his campaign to spend more than four times as much as Husted's so far, according to Federal Election Commission filings.

Despite all of that, Brown is still swimming upstream in a state that has become solidly red over the past few election cycles.

The word "competitive" is rarely used to describe statewide races in a place as red as South Carolina, but the death of longtime incumbent Sen. Lindsey Graham in July has set up what could be the Palmetto State's first tight Senate race in a generation.

Graham's sister, Darline Graham, was appointed to finish the rest of his term and is now running for a full six-year term. Her opponent is Democrat Annie Andrews, a pediatrician who has staked out several policy positions that reflect the state's conservatism, including support for the Second Amendment, tax cuts and strong immigration enforcement.

Republicans have comfortably won every Senate election in South Carolina since the early 2000s, but Trump's declining approval rating in the state and apparent concerns about Graham's lack of experience have likely contributed to making this a much closer race. Recent polls have shown Andrews trailing by as little as a single point, though forecasters still list the state as a leaning in Republican's direction.

Republicans haven't lost a statewide election in the Lone Star State in more than three decades, but forecasters say Democratic state lawmaker James Talarico has a chance of ending that streak in November.

His Republican opponent is Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who defeated longtime incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in a tightly contested and often contentious Republican primary. Paxton has faced serious legal issues during his tenure as Texas's top law enforcement official, including accusations of corruption that led the state House to impeach him in 2023. The state Senate later acquitted him on all articles it considered.

Polls have consistently shown a tight contest , with a good number finding Talarico leading by a small margin.

articles.title: Haley Stevens endorses Mike Rogers, ditches far-left Abdul El-Sayed
articles.summary: Unsurprisingly, Democrats are furious, and are roundly denouncing her as a traitor.
articles.body:
With the hours counting down before tomorrow’s midterm elections, there was a huge development in my home state of Michigan this weekend. Exhibiting a stunning rejection of leftist Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, Rep. Haley Stevens has unexpectedly endorsed Mike Rogers, the Republican candidate, in that Senate race.

Her announcement, posted to X on Sunday afternoon, followed days of escalating hostilities with El-Sayed, who defeated Stevens in the Democratic Senate primary. She initially endorsed her fellow Democrat, but then Stevens’s fiancé, Jason Turkish, stated last week he could not vote for El-Sayed, citing the candidate’s insufficient distance from Hasan Piker, Cenk Uygur and other unrelenting progressive critics of Israel.

That prompted El-Sayed to disinvite Stevens from all future campaign events; Rogers clearly sensed an opportunity, and secured Stevens’s support after reaching out to her.

Unsurprisingly, Democrats are furious, and are roundly denouncing her as a traitor. Her congressional staff is resigning en masse , apparently blindsided by the reversal. Even moderate liberal commentators who had preferred Stevens over El-Sayed in the primary are furious with her. Neera Tanden, a Democratic consultant who often feuds with the left wing of her party, accused Stevens of betraying “all of her supporters.” Activist David Hogg wrote that everyone who had backed Stevens over El-Sayed should apologize and condemn her . And commentator Matthew Yglesias wrote that he was very mad at Stevens.

And you know what? This all strikes me as a bit much. Take a chill pill, Dems: You are not owed the enthusiastic support of Haley Stevens when you select a candidate like El-Sayed.

And I get it, it of course matters a great deal which party controls the Senate, and thus individual races have extremely high stakes. Pro-Trump Americans want Republican majorities to protect them from bad Democratic policies, and anti-Trump Americans want the reverse. The country’s extremely defective two-party system, in which we are constantly called upon to compromise our own personal values and select the lesser of two evils, is on full display here.

But everyone slamming Stevens as some kind of traitor should know this: unshakeable, ironclad loyalty to one’s own political party is not a virtue. I would much prefer to live under a system in which Republicans and Democrats were more likely to buck their own parties and say that supporting such and such a person is outside the bounds of what can reasonably be expected.

It’s encouraging, for example, that Karl Rove has refused to vote for Bo French, the nominee for Texas Railroad Commissioner and an unapologetic anti-Indian racist . It would be better for the country if more Republicans followed his example — and if they similarly punished their Senate nominee, the manifestly corrupt Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.

I said all last week that I wanted Vivek Ramaswamy to get his comeuppance over that terrible ad, even though I largely agree with his policies. Well guess, what. The same should be true for Democrats.

And I know that El-Sayed does not appear to be corrupt or racist, and some of the allegations of anti-Semitism leveled against him are unfair : criticisms of the government of Israel are not synonymous with attacks on Jewish people. That said, he is an extremely far-left political candidate — a socialist in all but name — who thought it was a good idea to campaign with Piker, a communist sympathizer with a long track record of evincing support for terrorist groups . El-Sayed previously derided President Obama, who enacted an extremely progressive policy agenda, as “ fairly centrist, middle-of-the-road .” Democratic primary voters are free to pick leftists to be their candidates, but normal Democrats should not feel bound by those choices. Socialism, even socialism-lite, should always be viewed as a bridge too far, because it is a ruinous ideology that produces poverty and authoritarianism .

Now it’s true that Stevens appears to be doing this largely for reasons of personal spite rather than some ideological opposition to El-Sayed’s economic agenda, so I wouldn’t exactly nominate her for a Profiles in Courage Award. But the tendency to lash out at political figures who exercise a degree of independence and brand them as traitors is melodramatic at best. And it always goes only one way. Liz Cheney is celebrated for betraying the Republican Party, and Stevens is denounced for betraying the Democratic Party. That doesn’t seem right to me.

Now, as for El-Sayed: He is running well behind the Democratic Party’s gubernatorial nominee, Jocelyn Benson, which suggests to me that Stevens is not the only Michigan Democrat feeling uncomfortable about him. We will find out tomorrow. Or maybe Wednesday, depending on how the counting goes.

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.title: The 119th Congress did more by making government do less
articles.summary: In an op-ed, House Republican Conference Chairwoman Lisa McClain argues that the 119th Congress focused on reducing federal authority through record-breaking regulatory repeals, tax extensions, and border security measures.
articles.body:
Washington has a peculiar definition of progress. A new program is an accomplishment. A new regulation is action. A new federal office means somebody is finally doing something. That is why some of the most important work Republicans did this Congress involved undoing that so-called “progress.”

For decades, Washington accumulated authority one seemingly reasonable decision at a time. Congress delegated power to an agency full of faceless bureaucrats. The agency wrote a rule. The rule became another permit to obtain, expense to absorb, or decision somebody in Washington had already made for you.

Government grows quietly that way. Freedom disappears just as quietly. House Republicans of the 119th Congress came to Washington with the idea that the most consequential thing government can do is return freedom to the American people. Yes, we passed over 900 pieces of legislation this Congress, the second most in U.S. history, but that matters much less than what changed once the votes were cast.

House Republicans have overturned 23 federal rules through the Congressional Review Act, the most in history and more successful repeals than every previous Congress combined. In one session, we have turned a little-used oversight law into one of Washington’s most powerful tools for permanently returning authority from federal regulators to the people they regulate.

Washington is accustomed to ratchets that turn in one direction. Government expands, the bureaucracy adjusts, and everyone learns to live with the new baseline. We turned the ratchet backward.

Democrats would have let the 2017 tax cuts expire and taken more money out of Americans’ pockets. We made them permanent, cut taxes on tips and overtime, delivered new relief for seniors, and restored incentives to invest and build in America.

Americans have already claimed more than $82 billion in individual tax relief. Over the decade, the tax changes we enacted are projected to give $4.6 trillion back to families and businesses, and the laws enacted cut projected federal spending by roughly $1.1 trillion, meaning Washington will take less of Americans’ money.

People take bigger chances when they know more of the reward will still belong to them. That is how opportunity compounds and how countries grow. But opportunity can only flourish where freedom is protected by order and the rules still mean something.

A limited government is not a weak government. It does a smaller number of things, and it does the essential ones well. It must defend the country, enforce the law, protect basic rights, and establish rules that allow a free society to function.

Securing a nation’s borders is among the most basic responsibilities that government has. Democrats chose to dismantle our border and turn lawlessness into policy. Republicans flipped the script and have not allowed a single illegal immigrant to be released into the country in 16 months.

This Congress put the philosophy of limited government into practice across the economy. We gave small businesses tax certainty to hire and invest. We cleared regulatory barriers so manufacturers can expand, unleashed more American energy, and made it easier to build.

None of these policies determines what Americans must do with their lives. They expand what Americans are free to do for themselves.

The alternative is government by permission slip. Washington chooses which industries deserve to grow, which products people may buy, which energy sources are acceptable, and how much of a worker’s success belongs to somebody else. There needs to be a line between the power government is granted by the people, and the freedom Americans deserve to keep.

That is the foundation the 119th Congress has spent two years laying.

A foundation is not glamorous. Nobody walks through a finished house admiring the concrete underneath it, but everything built above depends on whether the foundation is strong.

Tax certainty. Regulatory relief. A secure border. American energy. Lower crime. More room to work, build and invest. These are not the finished house. They are what makes everything that comes next possible.

I don’t call the 119th Congress the most successful because of the paper it produced. I say it because we changed the direction of the country. Washington has enough monuments to what government can build. We spent this Congress creating room for what Americans can build instead.

The government does not know what your life should look like. Neither do I, and that’s precisely the point — you do.

Lisa McClain is chairwoman of the House Republican Conference.

articles.title: House Dems demand Haley Stevens' exile as Jeffries reveals deadline on deciding her fate
articles.summary: House Democratic leaders are considering action against Haley Stevens after her surprise endorsement of Mike Rogers in the Michigan Senate race over Abdul El-Sayed.
articles.body: House Democratic leaders are holding off on deciding whether to punish Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., after she endorsed a Republican in Michigan's Senate race, drawing calls from fellow Democrats for her removal from the party's House caucus. Stevens endorsed former Rep. Mike Rogers, R-Mich., over Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official, on Nov. 1 — just two days before Tuesday's midterm elections. The decision prompted sharp criticism from Democrats, including lawmakers who want Stevens expelled from the House Democratic Caucus, but party leaders are waiting until after the elections to address her future. HALEY STEVENS RIPPED BY FELLOW DEMS FOR REFUSING TO EXPLICITLY BACK EL-SAYED: 'STAY THE F--- OFF TELEVISION' A senior Democratic aide told Fox News Digital that House Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., would likely support House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., in his response to Stevens' endorsement. HALEY STEVENS' FIANCE HAMMERS EL-SAYED, SAYS HE'LL VOTE FOR ROGERS "Haley Stevens made a terrible decision, blindsided everyone and isolated herself from the House Democratic caucus. We will have a discussion about appropriate next steps upon our return," Jeffries told POLITICO. Spokespeople for Jeffries and Aguilar did not respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment. Stevens, a four-term lawmaker, is leaving Congress at the end of the year after narrowly losing Michigan's Democratic Senate primary to El-Sayed. Since her loss, Stevens has taken a lukewarm approach to supporting El-Sayed’s campaign while also criticizing his approach to Israel and Jewish and Black voters. BLACK VOTERS, JEWISH DEMOCRATS IN MICHIGAN WARY OF VOTING FOR EL-SAYED, SAY 'HE'S TAKING ADVANTAGE' That fragile peace ruptured over the weekend when El-Sayed’s campaign publicly asked Stevens to abstain from appearing at any of his events even after she said she would attend church with him and Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., in a bid to mobilize Black voters. Stevens apparently blindsided fellow Democrats when she then appeared at another church alongside Rogers and his wife and subsequently endorsed the Republican ahead of Election Day. EL-SAYED'S PAST MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD COMMENTS RAISE RED FLAGS AS HE EYES POWERFUL ROLE Rep. Debbie Dingell, D-Mich., said during a Sunday appearance on CNN that Stevens had reassured her "multiple times" over the weekend that she would not endorse Rogers. "I don't know what changed between late Saturday and Sunday morning," Dingell said during another CNN appearance Monday. And the endorsement also spurred her ouster from the Michigan state Democratic Party. Michigan Democratic Party Chairman Curtis Hertel wrote on X that Stevens "is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future" after she backed Rogers. In the House, Democratic officials, such as Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., have already called for Stevens’ removal. "Deplorable and embarrassing. Capitulating to fascism, Islamophobia, racism and the policies hurting everyday Americans makes you unfit to serve with the Democratic caucus," Ramirez wrote on X. "Shame on Haley Stevens. She must be removed from the caucus." HALEY STEVENS CONDEMNS HASAN PIKER BUT RALLIES BEHIND EL-SAYED AFTER NARROW PRIMARY LOSS Ramirez did not respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment. Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., echoed Ramirez’s claim and added that Stevens "has no place in our party," according to POLITICO. Vocal organizations aligned with the Democratic Party, such as the IfNotNow movement, have also formally called on the congresswoman to be removed from the caucus, calling her endorsement a betrayal to the party. "As national organizations representing Jewish, Muslim, and Democratic voters opposed to Donald Trump's war on Iran, which is responsible for the rising costs of gas and groceries and an affordability crisis that is taking a heavy toll on working families at a time when the future of our democracy is at stake," the organization said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital. "We call on House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries to expel Congresswoman Stevens from the Democratic Caucus and strip her of her committee assignments." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP If Stevens was removed from the caucus, she would no longer be able to attend its weekly meetings in the U.S. Capitol. Democrats could also pursue action against her committee assignments, though the process and authority for doing so would need to be determined under the applicable caucus and House rules. And it appears Stevens' staff has also shunned her over the endorsement. When Fox News Digital reached out to her office for comment on the backlash from House Democrats, an automated response from her communications director said he is "no longer with the Office of Congresswoman Haley Stevens" as of Nov. 1, the day she backed Rogers.

articles.title: ‘Despicable’: Haley Stevens blasted by Dems after endorsing Mike Rogers
articles.summary: Stevens is entitled to disagree with El-Sayed, but repeatedly creating headlines that undermine your own party’s nominee days before an election that could decide the balance of power in the Senate is absurd.
articles.body:
Well, it’s official. After weeks of publicly questioning Abdul El-Sayed, Congresswoman Haley Stevens has now endorsed his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers. And she did it less than 48 hours before Election Day .

This is a very shameless display of political opportunism. She didn’t all of a sudden develop some admiration for a man she previously criticized as a “rubber stamp for Donald Trump’s dangerous agenda.” What she did with this endorsement is demonstrate how little her words and everything she claims to stand for are worth, because we don’t have to guess what Stevens thought about Mike Rogers. We have the receipts from her own X account.

In August : “Mike Rogers will be another rubber stamp for Donald Trump’s dangerous agenda.”

In June : “Mike Rogers’ record on LGBTQ+ rights is repulsive. He has no business representing Michiganders.”

In April : She called Rogers “MAGA Mike” and described him as “disgraceful,” pointing to controversy surrounding his outreach team’s hiring of students who praised Hitler.

And let me not forget this one, where she said: “Mike Rogers can’t hide his terrible record on abortion rights.”

Now, remember, this is the same Stevens who repeatedly said she would support the Democratic ticket after losing the primary in August. This is the same woman who outspent El-Sayed 12 to 1 and still lost. Her endorsement, after losing, has come with some pretty significant caveats, and no display of public unity on the same stage.

Instead of just saying she doesn’t endorse El-Sayed from the start, she is suggesting an independent ad from Cenk Uygur’s Rebellion PAC criticizing U.S. military aid to Israel and connecting it to Americans’ rising grocery bills is the reason why her support for El-Sayed has collapsed. El-Sayed has repeatedly distanced himself from the ad in question, telling a reporter : “That ad was not made by me and I do not agree with the contents of that ad.”

It seems she never really wanted to support El-Sayed. After Barack Obama’s Oct. 24 rally highlighted Democratic momentum in Michigan, Stevens appeared on CNN the following day, raising questions about El-Sayed’s campaign while sidestepping whether she was fully invested in helping him win.

On Oct. 26, she publicly criticized the PAC ad. At the same time, the El-Sayed campaign explicitly states : Ad not affiliated with campaign or Abdul. Two days later, her fiancé, Jason Turkish, attended a Mike Rogers event alongside Ted Cruz and endorsed Rogers, while Stevens continued telling CNN she planned to vote for El-Sayed.

Then, just two days before a planned joint church appearance with El-Sayed and Congressman Jim Clyburn, Stevens issued a lengthy statement demanding that El-Sayed disavow the ad. Her fiancé subsequently appeared on TMZ, suggesting she could possibly reconsider her endorsement.

El-Sayed’s campaign pushed back , saying he didn’t want her appearance to become a distraction. A statement from his team he released on X said: “Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago.”

His statement also reminded voters that AIPAC spent heavily trying to defeat him and supporting Stevens in that primary. Now Stevens has become the topic of conversation instead of the policies and the race.

Even Michigan State Senator Mallory McMorrow, who dropped out of the Democratic primary in July, seemed baffled : “I have no idea what the hell Haley Stevens is doing. This is a moment where we have to recognize the stakes.”

Lots of people even in Stevens’s own office are thoroughly confused. Her longtime chief of staff announced his resignation Sunday, saying multiple members of the team had also resigned. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer called her decision a “despicable betrayal.”

Stevens is entitled to disagree with El-Sayed, but repeatedly creating headlines that undermine your own party’s nominee days before an election that could decide the balance of power in the Senate is absurd.

The last-minute endorsement of a man you’ve criticized for everything from his abortion record to hiring antisemitic people to having a terrible record on LGBTQ rights is truly wild.

Stevens cannot spend months telling voters that control of the Senate is on the line and that you want to fight for health care reforms and many of the same policies of El-Sayed, then spend the final days publicly undermining the very candidate you need to get those policies to the finish line.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

articles.title: Kennedy Center to recognize Paul Anka, Andy Garcia, Barbara Mandrell at off-site Honors ceremony
articles.summary: Playwright David Mamet, songwriter Paul Anka, composer David Foster, actor Andy Garcia and country music singer Barbara Mandrell are poised to receive the Kennedy Center Honors this year at a ceremony that will be held off-site amid a legal battle over renovations and adding President Trump’s name to the performing arts institution. The Kennedy Center…
articles.body:
Playwright David Mamet, songwriter Paul Anka, composer David Foster, actor Andy Garcia and country music singer Barbara Mandrell are poised to receive the Kennedy Center Honors this year at a ceremony that will be held off-site amid a legal battle over renovations and adding President Trump’s name to the performing arts institution.

The Kennedy Center announced the honorees for its 49th annual awards Monday.

“We are recognizing amazing artists whose lifelong work has shaped American culture and inspired generations of audiences,” Trump said in a statement about this year’s recipients.

“We are proud to honor this year’s class and to continue a tradition that has defined the Center for nearly 50 years,” the president said.

The announcement comes at a perilous time for the Kennedy Center.

For the first time in its history, the Dec. 7 Honors gala will not be held inside the center itself — it’ll instead be hosted at the Capital One Arena in Washington.

Last month, Trump declined to commit to not demolishing the Washington entertainment hub as the legal fights over its name and a major renovation play out.

In 2025, Trump named himself the chair of the Kennedy Center’s board, firing several members and installing a handpicked slate of administration officials and allies.

In November of last year, the board voted to add the president’s name to the facade of the building. The move was later reversed by a federal judge.

Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex officio board member, has since led a legal challenge over the Kennedy Center changes.

The center’s board voted in September to close the main building for renovations, citing statements from its officials that it was “unsafe for continued occupancy.”

Last year’s Kennedy Center Honors — the first ceremony following Trump’s unprecedented overhaul — recognized artists including Sylvester Stallone, members of the band Kiss, Gloria Gaynor, George Strait and Michael Crawford. Trump also hosted the event .

articles.title: Mamdani threatens to sue Trump administration over alleged ICE use of New York City property
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) on Monday threatened to sue the Trump administration over Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) alleged use of city property. In a letter addressed to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, acting ICE Director David Venturella and ICE New York field office Director Kenneth Genalo, Mamdani states that he is…
articles.body:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) on Monday threatened to sue the Trump administration over Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) alleged use of city property.

In a letter addressed to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, acting ICE Director David Venturella and ICE New York field office Director Kenneth Genalo, Mamdani states that he is “deeply troubled by recent reports” of ICE officers “using property owned by the City of New York to stage enforcement operations.”

“This use of City property in furtherance of federal immigration enforcement is unauthorized and is therefore illegal, endangers City residents, and sows fear among those who seek to access City property,” the mayor said in his letter .

“If your agents continue any unauthorized use of these lots, New York City will take legal action to prevent this unlawful commandeering of City property,” Mamdani added.

Mamdani, one of the more prominent progressive figures in the Democratic Party, has pushed for the abolition of ICE .

In mid-October , Mamdani and other New York Democratic leaders pushed for the city’s private parking lot owners to bar ICE from their properties.

“In solidarity with immigrant New Yorkers and in our shared commitment to the City we love, we ask that you do not rent, lend or otherwise make your property available to ICE as a staging area for its enforcement operations,” the mayor wrote in a letter to owners and operators of these properties.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) were among more than 100 elected officials who signed on to Mamdani’s earlier letter.

The Hill has reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment.

articles.title: Adam Hamilton responds to Trump’s ‘perverted pastor’ remarks in Kansas
articles.summary: Kansas Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton said it was “pathetic” for President Trump to call him a “perverted pastor” at a Sunday rally in support of Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.). “I think it’s sad, it’s pathetic to be calling a pastor a pervert and all the things that he’s been saying,” Hamilton told NewsNation’s Mills…
articles.body:
Kansas Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton said it was “pathetic” for President Trump to call him a “perverted pastor” at a Sunday rally in support of Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.).

“I think it’s sad, it’s pathetic to be calling a pastor a pervert and all the things that he’s been saying,” Hamilton told NewsNation’s Mills Hayes on Monday.

Hamilton said he took Trump’s Sunday insults , which echoed attacks the president made against Hamilton at another October rally , as an “honor.” The Democrat added he is praying for both Trump and Marshall.

Hamilton is locked in a tight race that could make him the first Democrat to represent Kansas in the upper chamber in nearly a century.

“I’ll just say, it doesn’t bother me,” Hamilton added of Trump’s remark. “I feel like that says more about him than it says about me.”

Hamilton said Trump — who hit Hamilton over his support for transgender rights — held the rally two days before Election Day to boost the Republican in a race most did not expect to be competitive just a few months ago.

The president originally canceled the rally but ended up appearing anyway after forcefully pushing back on reporters questioning his motive for the cancellation.

“He’s come here at the end of a long day, and he’s come here desperately trying to save my opponent, Roger Marshall, and I don’t think that’s going to happen,” Hamilton said.

Hamilton has consistently portrayed himself as a centrist as he tries to win in a state Trump carried by more than 16 points two years ago. Despite the conflict, Hamilton said he will work with the president on anything that would benefit Kansans.

“Anything the president wants to do that’s good for the people of Kansas, I will be his best partner here,” Hamilton said.

Hamilton, the longtime pastor for one of the largest United Methodist churches in the nation, said there is no need to be squeamish over his ties to the church and that he believes the separation of church and state is “very important.” A supporter of same-sex marriage and abortion rights, Hamilton also addressed concerns from Christians about his views on the issues.

“There’s room for people to have differences of opinion on things,” Hamilton said. “If you’re not in favor of same-sex marriage, then be who you are. But do it lovingly.”

As for his chances of winning, Hamilton said he is “cautiously optimistic.”

“I do think we have a really good chance to win on election night,” the pastor said. “It’s going to be fun.”

articles.title: Mike Rogers dishes on how shock Haley Stevens endorsement unfolded hours before Election Day
articles.summary: GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers defended Dem Rep Haley Stevens as top Democrats erupted over her decision to cross party lines and endorse him over Abdul El-Sayed just before Election Day.
articles.body: Michigan Republican U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers praised Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens for putting America ahead of her party Monday while accusing Democrats of viciously attacking the congresswoman after she stunned her party by endorsing him over Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed. Rogers told Brian Kilmeade on the "Brian Kilmeade Show" that Stevens’ endorsement "flipped this thing upside down," saying the congresswoman called him Sunday morning while he was on his way to church before ultimately deciding to publicly back his campaign following her bruising primary loss to El-Sayed. "This is a congresswoman who just stood up and said, 'America is more important than my party right now,'" Rogers said. "And we cannot elect somebody who is so anti-Jewish, who is divisive, who's angry, who was mean about his politics. It's just the wrong thing to do." EL SAYED'S LEFT-WING ALLIES ATTACK 'EVIL' STEVENS AFTER BOMBSHELL ROGERS ENDORSEMENT Rogers' comments came as Fox News reported Monday that Stevens' endorsement triggered backlash from top Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif. Schumer called the move a "despicable betrayal," while Pelosi accused Stevens of "dangerously" betraying Michigan families by backing Rogers. The endorsement marked a dramatic break for Stevens, who had stopped short of explicitly endorsing El-Sayed in the weeks after losing the Democratic primary but continued to publicly align herself with the party. During an October CNN interview, Stevens was repeatedly pressed on whether she supported El-Sayed and declined to explicitly say she endorsed him, instead stressing that she was "still on the team" and planned to support Democrats on the ballot. The tensions between the former primary rivals had been building in the closing stretch of the race. Stevens pressed El-Sayed to condemn an outside group's ad linking U.S. support for Israel to higher grocery prices, which she called antisemitic, before El-Sayed's campaign asked her to stay away from its remaining campaign events. El-Sayed said his campaign did not produce the ad and that he disagreed with its contents. MICHIGAN DEMOCRAT HALEY STEVENS BACKS EL-SAYED AFTER NARROW PRIMARY DEFEAT, CALLS SOCIALISM ‘DANGEROUS’ Meanwhile, days before she publicly endorsed Rogers, Stevens' fiancé, Jason Turkish, had already broken with the Democratic nominee. Turkish, a Jewish Michigan attorney and registered Democrat, told reporters at a Rogers campaign event that he planned to vote for the Republican, arguing that El-Sayed's rhetoric on Israel had made the Jewish community "less safe." Turkish described his decision as "putting country before party." Still, even hours before the endorsement, Stevens appeared to be denying that she planned to back Rogers. Fox News Digital reported Monday that Rep. Debbie Dingell, D-Mich., said she spoke with Stevens around midnight Saturday and was told reports of an impending Rogers endorsement were a "rumor" and "not true." However, hours later, Stevens was standing alongside Rogers at a Detroit church service, where she ultimately announced she would cross party lines and endorse him over El-Sayed. "We didn't know what was going to happen. We were driving to the church yesterday morning when the call came in," Rogers said. "I just invited her to come in. She decided between when she got in the car and she got to the church, she was going to not only withdraw the endorsement, but endorse me." articles.title: El-Sayed's silence over mom's FBI questioning raises transparency concerns
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed's mother was questioned by the FBI after a 2004 raid on the Islamic American Relief Agency, but the Senate candidate says he has no ties.
articles.body: Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is facing renewed scrutiny from Republican critics over his mother's questioning by federal investigators more than two decades ago as part of an investigation into an Islamic charity where she worked. El-Sayed's Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, R-Mich., accused the Democratic candidate of misleading Michigan voters about his views on the Muslim Brotherhood, pointing to reported associations involving members of El-Sayed's family. El-Sayed previously told Fox News that he has "never been" and will "never be" a member of the Muslim Brotherhood. Fox News Digital is not aware of any direct ties between El-Sayed and the organization. El-Sayed's campaign did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. CONTROVERSY OVER ABDUL EL-SAYED'S FAMILY TIES TO MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD IGNORED, DOWNPLAYED BY LIBERAL MEDIA "Michiganders cannot trust Abdul El-Sayed. He lies about his physician credentials, his family life, and about how much his disastrous policies will cost Michigan's families," a spokesperson for Rogers told Fox News Digital. "Tell the truth, Abdul." El-Sayed has not publicly addressed the details of his mother's questioning by federal investigators or the raid on the offices of the Islamic charity where she worked since the Washington Free Beacon resurfaced the reports last month. Federal authorities raided the Missouri office of the Islamic American Relief Agency (IARA), where El-Sayed's mother, Fatten Elkomy, worked in 2004, according to the Columbia Daily Tribune. The newspaper reported that federal agents questioned Elkomy for approximately three hours during the investigation. In 2008, IARA was shut down by the federal government in connection with alleged violations of federal sanctions and terrorism-related financing restrictions, including allegations involving funding for Islamic militants in Afghanistan and terrorist groups such as the Taliban and al Qaeda. Elkomy was not charged in connection with the investigation, according to multiple reports. Fox News Digital has found no evidence that she facilitated transfers of funds to terrorist organizations. The U.S. Treasury Department did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment about the government's findings concerning IARA's alleged connections to the Muslim Brotherhood or why Elkomy was questioned by federal investigators. TRUMP LINKS MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE ABDUL EL-SAYED TO MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD: 'HE'S A CON MAN' During his Senate campaign, El-Sayed has sought to distance himself from his mother's reported political associations, emphasizing that she did not raise him. El-Sayed was raised in Michigan by his father and stepmother after his parents divorced when he was 3. "I have no ties. We have no ties," El-Sayed told NBC's Tom Llamas in October. "I have never had these conversations with my mother, I wasn't raised by my mother." The scrutiny of El-Sayed extended to the candidate's fundraisers and campaign events with Islamic leaders, some of whom have reported ties to the Muslim Brotherhood or have been accused of making antisemitic or hateful remarks. The controversy has also included El-Sayed's campaign appearances with left-wing streamer Hasan Piker. His former Democratic primary opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., endorsed Rogers on Sunday, citing concerns about El-Sayed's approach to the safety of Michigan's Jewish community and his repeated campaign appearances with Piker, who previously said, "America deserved 9/11." "I don't like a democratic nominee for U.S. senate campaigning and standing with someone who's saying that America deserved 9/11," Stevens said during a CNN interview Sunday night. El-Sayed declined to comment on Piker's remarks during an April interview with POLITICO but later disavowed them during an August appearance on NBC's "Meet the Press." EL-SAYED ERUPTS AT GOP RIVAL OVER MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD ACCUSATIONS IN FIERY SENATE DEBATE Amy Mek, founder of the RAIR Foundation, a nonprofit organization focused on investigating groups it identifies as connected to terrorism, echoed Rogers' concerns about national security and El-Sayed's silence in a statement to Fox News Digital. Mek, who previously testified before Congress about terrorism-related threats in the United States, told Fox News Digital that she believes El-Sayed's silence on his mother's questioning reflects political considerations. She also pointed to social media posts by El-Sayed's half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, who wrote on X in 2012 that members of their family have "long been" members of the Muslim Brotherhood. Abdelhadi later recalled her family's fear of FBI surveillance in a 2016 article titled, "Queer, Muslim, and Unwelcome at the 'New Stonewall.'" articles.title: Trump to remove Rwanda and South Africa from US trade deal
articles.summary: The move comes barely a week after Rwanda's defence ministry was hit with sanctions by the US Treasury.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has notified Congress of his intention to remove South Africa and Rwanda from a preferential trade programme, from 1 January 2027.

The African Growth and Opportunity Act (Agoa) allows eligible African countries to export thousands of products to the US duty-free.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement that an annual review had found that both countries were engaging in practices inconsistent with the programme's eligibility requirements.

He added that the Trump administration had additionally notified the two countries of the decision.

The Trump administration cited barriers to US trade and investment, as well as concerns over national security and foreign policy interests in the region.

In Rwanda's case, Washington also raised concerns about human rights, political pluralism, the rule of law and workers' rights.

The move comes barely a week after Rwanda's defence ministry was hit with sanctions by US Treasury for its alleged role in the armed rebellion in eastern DR Congo.

The US Treasury said Rwanda's defence ministry directed thousands of troops to fight alongside M23 rebels in eastern DR Congo, providing weapons, equipment, logistics and training.

For South Africa, the US additionally pointed to corruption.

"The Trump administration is working to ensure our African partners take the necessary steps to meet the eligibility criteria," Greer said.

The announcement comes amid strained relations between Washington and both countries, with the proposed termination threatening their access to preferential trade arrangements with the US.

Last year, Trump accused South Africa of white genocide in a meeting with President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White House and launched a US refugee pathway for Afrikaners.

US Ambassador to South Africa Leo Brent Bozell III said it was regrettable that South African policies led to its termination from Agoa.

"This was a predictable and preventable outcome resulting from the rejection by South Africa's government of real concerns raised by the US," he wrote on X.

The word is seen in various online communities spanning health, AI and beauty. The most notable of the initial version was looksmaxing. Before going viral, the word was often used amongst young men, but now, the term can be aspirational, earnest or mocking depending on how it is used.

The announcement garnered mixed reactions online, with some people criticizing the choice. The word of the year is intended to reflect the collective journey of the year. Other top choices were affordability, data center, unc and odyssey.

Maxxing was chosen because it captures the 2026 urge to keep pushing harder while also giving an opportunity to poke fun at ourselves when optimizing our lives feels silly.

articles.title: Adults 23-26 are America’s least religious age group: Study
articles.summary: The findings come amid media reports of a possible religious revival among young Americans, especially conservative men.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — More U.S. adults are attending religious services than during the pandemic, but the country’s youngest adults differ on religion depending on when they were born, according to new surveys conducted by the Pew Research Center.

Among adults ages 18-22, around 41 percent said they attend services at least once or twice a month, compared with 33 percent of all U.S. adults. But among those slightly older, between the ages of 23-26, that share is 27 percent, among the lowest of any group.

Attendance is up, but signs of religious revival limited

The findings come amid media reports of a possible religious revival among young Americans, especially young conservative men. An April Gallup poll showed more young men in the U.S. saying religion was “very important” in their lives than young women. President Trump has also often spoken of a revival in religiosity among young people in the U.S.

According to Pew , there was a sharp rise in the share of U.S. adults who said religion was gaining influence in American life between 2024 and 2025.

Pew’s data offers only partial support of that idea. While adults aged 18-22 report spending more time attending services, they report praying less and rank religion as a less important priority, according to the surveys. They are also no more religious than people the same age were in 2014, and less religious than people that age were in 2007.

The second-youngest group of adults surveyed, those between 23 and 26, were the least religious age group on all the ways the researchers used to measure religiousness, including how often they prayed, how important they said religion was in their lives and whether they identified with a religion.

For the first time in the organization’s survey, men aged 18-22 reported going to services more often than women, though 35 percent of women in that age group report attending services at least monthly, which is more than women born in the 1990s and early 2000s.

Among the youngest Republicans in the 18-22 age group, 55 percent said they attended at least monthly, which made up a higher share than any other age group of Republicans, except the oldest group. The youngest Democrats surveyed also reported attending more often than Democrats born between the 1970s and the early 2000s.

Across all U.S. adults, religion has held steady since 2020 after experiencing a long decline. A June survey found 34 percent of people surveyed had attended services in person in the past month and 45 percent said they had attended in person or watched online or on TV, which both were the highest reported figures since Pew between asking in July 2020.

Pew: Religiosity among young Americans could indicate ‘turning point’ — or blip

Pew says the surveys paint “a complicated picture” of religion among young U.S. adults.

In the past, young adults who entered adulthood with relatively high levels of religious involvement tended to become less religious over time. Pew says it can’t yet tell if that’s also what the current numbers represent.

“Time will tell whether the relatively high religiousness of today’s youngest adults is a turning point or a blip in the data,” the study concluded.

articles.title: Pentagon's top spies tasked with 'no-fail' mission as Hegseth puts foreign midterm meddling in crosshairs
articles.summary: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth's September directive mobilizes the entire Defense Intelligence Enterprise for midterm election security overseas.
articles.body: Ever since the 2016 presidential election that first got President Donald Trump elected and the ensuing Russiagate scandal, there has been increased scrutiny on foreign meddling in U.S. elections and threats to the American voting system. Now, 10 years later, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is directing his entire intelligence and spy forces to ensure foreign adversaries do not interfere in Tuesday's midterms. The Pentagon chief has ordered America's military intelligence and cyber agencies to mobilize against foreign threats to the 2026 elections by directing his department's sprawling intelligence apparatus to make election security a priority in what he calls a "no-fail mission." The September directive reaches beyond U.S. Cyber Command and the National Security Agency, instructing the entire Defense Intelligence Enterprise — including agencies responsible for military and geospatial intelligence — to "mobilize every authorized asset, capability, and partnership" against foreign election threats. HOW TO WATCH CRITICAL 2026 MIDTERM ELECTION RACES IN TX, OH, MI, WI, GA, IA, NV, ME AND FL The order puts some of the military's most sophisticated intelligence capabilities behind a mission that has grown considerably since Russia's interference in the 2016 presidential election. But with Americans preparing to vote, the extent to which Hegseth's directive has changed the Pentagon's existing election-security operations remains unclear. The Department of War declined to provide Fox News Digital with additional details about how the order is being implemented. Cyber Command separately declined an interview request about its election-security efforts. In practice, the directive can mean military intelligence agencies are tasked with identifying foreign hackers or influence operations overseas, warning civilian agencies about threats headed toward U.S. targets and, when authorized, Cyber Command taking action against the foreign actors or infrastructure behind them. The military's role largely stops at the U.S. border: state and local officials run elections, while agencies such as the FBI and Department of Homeland Security handle the domestic side. The Pentagon's election security mission is not new. Cyber Command and NSA have spent years tracking and disrupting foreign threats around American elections, including operations targeting Russian actors during previous election cycles. The effort began taking its current shape ahead of the 2018 midterms, when the agencies formed a "Russia Small Group" focused on foreign interference. It later evolved into a joint Election Security Group, combining NSA's intelligence-gathering capabilities with Cyber Command's ability to conduct operations against foreign cyber threats. By 2022, then-Cyber Command and NSA chief Gen. Paul Nakasone was describing election security as an "enduring, no-fail mission" — language echoed by Hegseth four years later. "Rest assured, we were doing operations well before the midterms began, and we were doing operations likely on the day of the midterms," Nakasone said after the 2022 election, describing the military's role as "understanding your foreign adversaries and operating outside the United States." The agencies again established an Election Security Group for the 2024 presidential election, but whether that structure was recreated for this year's midterms has been less clear. Gen. Joshua Rudd, the current head of Cyber Command and NSA, told lawmakers in April that foreign interference was "reasonable to expect based on what we've seen in the past" and said his command was "postured and ready to support as required or tasked." He said at the time that he was unsure whether the Election Security Group had been reconvened. CHINA-LINKED HACKERS INFILTRATED US GOVERNMENT NETWORKS BEFORE FBI TAKEDOWN Five months later, Hegseth issued his department-wide directive, addressed not only to Cyber Command and NSA but also to the directors of the Defense Intelligence Agency and National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency. The order instructs military intelligence agencies to collect and analyze intelligence on foreign election threats while directing Cyber Command to use its existing authorities and capabilities to counter potential foreign cyber activity in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security. It does not publicly grant new authorities or establish a new election-security organization, instead reinforcing a mission the military has increasingly treated as an enduring responsibility. U.S. intelligence officials, meanwhile, say they have seen no evidence that a foreign adversary has attempted to interfere with voting machines, physical election infrastructure or the counting of votes ahead of Tuesday's midterms. Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn., the ranking member of the House Intelligence Committee, said last week that intelligence officials continue to see nothing contradicting that assessment, but urged Americans to remain "on high alert" for foreign disinformation, particularly as artificial intelligence makes such campaigns easier to spread. But officials continue to track foreign influence efforts from Russia, China and Iran, with Russia remaining the most active foreign influence threat, CNN reported Sunday. U.S. elections are attractive targets for foreign adversaries because the stakes extend far beyond who wins office: influencing American voters or undermining confidence in the process can shape U.S. policy, weaken public support for policies they oppose and deepen divisions without ever touching a voting machine. Lawmakers briefed on classified intelligence last month said Russia was using disinformation to target candidates and undermine confidence in the election, while China's influence efforts were more narrowly focused on candidates viewed as hostile to Beijing. The Pentagon's role focuses on threats originating overseas, while state and local officials administer elections and civilian federal agencies lead domestic election-security efforts. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Hegseth's directive makes that overseas mission a priority across the broader military intelligence enterprise, though the Pentagon has not disclosed whether it has resulted in additional personnel, resources or organizational changes ahead of Election Day.

articles.title: Hamilton calls Marshall medical debt video ‘desperate’
articles.summary: Kansas Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton called his opponent’s attempt to explain away his past lawsuits against indebted patients “desperate.” Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.), an obstetrician, recorded a video disputing claims that he sued more than 700 former patients for overdue medical bills, including some for debts as low as $101. Hamilton said the video…
articles.body:
Kansas Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton called his opponent’s attempt to explain away his past lawsuits against indebted patients “desperate.”

Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.), an obstetrician, recorded a video disputing claims that he sued more than 700 former patients for overdue medical bills, including some for debts as low as $101. Hamilton said the video misled voters over his former medical practice’s debt-collection efforts.

“It felt like to me that he was desperately trying to explain away something,” Hamilton told NewsNation’s Mills Hayes on Monday.

The New York Times reported in September that Marshall filed the suits against more than 700 patients over the span of his medical career in an effort to collect on overdue medical bills. Patients were arrested in 81 cases after missing court appearances, according to records reviewed by the Times.

In a video recorded and produced by the senator without the help of his campaign, Marshall said he occasionally handed overdue bills to a collection agency to “keep the lights on.”

“My involvement in any patient’s account ended the minute it was turned over to an outside agency,” Marshall said . “I never had anyone arrested.”

The Times reported that about half of the lawsuits were filed in the senator’s name and that his lawyers repeatedly requested arrest warrants to be issued in the cases, but Marshall holds that he regularly worked without pay to help his patients.

“When I practiced as a small town OB doc, often serving as the only OB in the middle of 40,000 people, my wife and I decided to take care of everyone regardless of their ability to pay,” Marshall claimed in the video . “We wrote off hundreds of bills monthly and one in every five patients received free care.”

Hamilton claimed Marshall’s personal attorney filed the lawsuits and that the Senator had a say in how aggressively they were pursued.

“The reality is, if you actually check the facts, he’s not telling the truth,” Hamilton said.

articles.title: Marshall cuts rogue ad on medical debt lawsuits
articles.summary: Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) released a new campaign ad this past weekend responding to attacks toward him over his medical debt lawsuits against former patients, reportedly bucking his campaign team’s guidance. “When I practiced as a small-town OB doc [obstetrician], often serving as the only OB in the middle of 40,000 people, my wife and…
articles.body:
Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) released a new campaign ad this past weekend responding to attacks toward him over his medical debt lawsuits against former patients, reportedly bucking his campaign team’s guidance.

“When I practiced as a small-town OB doc [obstetrician], often serving as the only OB in the middle of 40,000 people, my wife and I decided to take care of everyone, regardless of their ability to pay,” Marshall, dressed in a red button-up shirt while resting on a wooden fence, said in the minute-long ad.

“We wrote off hundreds of bills monthly, and one of every five patients received precare,” he continued. “Now, to ensure that 40,000 Kansans would still have access to care, we did have to keep the lights on. So we occasionally handed some accounts over to a collection agency, just like nearly every private medical practice does.”

Marshall said Kansas’s bill of rights “ensures that no one can go to prison because of indebtedness, and I would never wish that on any patient.”

He added that his “involvement in any patients’ account ended the minute it was turned over to an outside agency” and that he never called for anyone’s arrest.

“Kansas deserves to know the truth, and now you do,” he said before asking for Kansans’ votes on Tuesday.

The senator was a practicing OB-GYN until 2016, when he was elected to Congress.

Marshall filed lawsuits against more than 700 patients seeking payments on their medical debt during his time as a physician, The New York Times reported in September . At least 81 patients were arrested for missing court dates, while others faced wage garnishments.

The Kansas Republican wanted to respond to attacks from Kansas Senate candidate Adam Hamilton (D) with a new ad, four people with knowledge of the matter told the Times . His campaign’s top advisers urged him not to release the ad and suggested he focus on Hamilton’s record on immigration.

But the senator arranged for his own film crew to record and release the ad without the knowledge of at least some of his top aides, the outlet reported.

Some campaign advisers moved to stop the ad from being released, but Marshall sent it to people outside the campaign, two people briefed on Marshall’s text exchanges told the Times.

“I would have been glad to put it out much, much sooner,” Marshall told The Wall Street Journal . “Constantly on the trail, I’ll have town halls, meetings with people here and they ask me, will you explain it to me? And so I keep explaining it everywhere I go, and people just requested a video one time, so we get it.”

Marshall previously sent a cease-and-desist letter to Hamilton in September after the Democrat released an ad that focused on a woman who was sued over medical debts to Marshall. That woman, Meischa Zimmerman, said she was arrested after failing to make a monthly payment of $50 toward her medical debt to Marshall.

Zimmerman, whose story has drawn attention as the campaign neared Election Day, filed a class-action lawsuit against Marshall and his medical practice on Thursday, The Washington Post reported . She accused Marshall of setting up a “callous and predatory” debt collection scheme that took advantage of her and other patients.

Republicans fear that the lawsuits could cause the “ perfect storm ” that would open Kansas up to having a Democratic senator for the first time in almost a century. President Trump defended Marshall earlier this month, saying he was “given a ‘bum rap’ because he was mandated by Law to request money owed from patients.”
