articles.title: Ahead of Election Day, Trump sets the stage for potential Republican losses
articles.summary: President Donald Trump acknowledged historical trends against the president’s party in midterm elections, saying Monday, “We gave this a very strong shot.”
articles.body: In an election-eve speech at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, President Donald Trump said Republicans “gave this a very strong shot” while acknowledging that historically, the president’s party “doesn’t win the midterms.” “This is the last day before the midterm elections — the most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime,” Trump said Monday in his final major speech before the midterm elections Tuesday. “The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history. These are the most dangerous candidates ever put up.” Although a White House official had said in advance that the speech would represent Trump’s “closing message” before voters make their final trips to the polls, Trump spent most of his remarks speaking about the Reflecting Pool. Trump announced the Reflecting Pool will reopen after months of repairs and talked about other renovation projects he has ordered around Washington, a key focus and fascination of his second term. Speaking about the election, he touted what he considered economic wins, saying that “personal incomes are the highest in history” and that “the poverty rate is at an all-time record low.” But, he said, “it all doesn’t matter if we’re going to be foolish and let people that hate our country win an election.” “If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election ... just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” he continued. “Now, that doesn’t happen, because usually, whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, good or bad, good president, great president, bad — for some reason, the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.” Trump derided Democratic candidates and falsely said some were jihadists or members of the Muslim Brotherhood. He said they are “all committed to the same radical agenda: open borders, raising your taxes by trillions of dollars, taking away your guns, transgender mutilation of your children, abolishing oil and natural gas, sending energy costs skyrocketing and opening the floodgates to millions of migrants from all over the world, hoping to get them to be able to vote.” Trump referred to Alaska’s Senate race and last week’s report by The New York Times that Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign and other Democrats recruited a candidate — Dan J. Sullivan — to run for the Senate with the same name as the incumbent. Peltola has denied having been aware of the reported scheme. “They got somebody named Dan Sullivan to run against Dan Sullivan,” Trump said. “It’s corrupt. It’s really a fraud, fraudulent election.” Asked by NBC News after his remarks whether he would consider resuming strikes on Iran after the election, Trump said, “No.” Trump closed out a 28-rally swing through the U.S. to campaign for Republican candidates Sunday. He traveled for 25 days in the final month of the campaign, visiting 19 states. He held his final rallies outside Washington on Sunday, with one in Kansas and the other in Iowa, both states with competitive Senate races. Trump is scheduled to participate in several tele-rallies for the midterms from Washington on Monday. On the final day of the 2018 midterm election cycle, by contrast, he held in-person rallies in three states. “We’ve got some big races tomorrow,” Trump said in his remarks. “I guess some of the voting has already gone on, but tomorrow’s Election Day, more traditional.” Asked Sunday why he chose to speak at the Reflecting Pool, Trump told reporters: “Just to show how beautiful it is. It’s been finished. It was vandalized badly. We have cameras all over the place now for the vandals.” On Monday, he stood next to a poster that said, “Back, and more beautiful than ever.” “We’re booming like we’ve never boomed before,” he said. “We’ve cleaned hundreds of sites of graffiti, fixed over 2,300 lighting fixtures in Washington, D.C., cleaned and renovated over 83 statues and fountains and monuments, removed hundreds of squalid homeless encampments.” In addition to the Reflecting Pool between the Lincoln Memorial and the World War II Memorial downtown, Trump highlighted other construction projects he launched, including the White House ballroom, a White House helipad, a new golf course in the city and a triumphal arch, among other projects. Trump appeared to joke at one point that the Reflecting Pool would be named after him. The Reflecting Pool has been closed since July after additional renovations had to be made when the bottom coating peeled and algae formed, tinting the water green. The National Park Service announced recently that it was extending the closure of the pool and the areas surrounding it until Nov. 20. After the initial renovation process began in June and it first reopened to the public, Trump accused multiple people of “destroying” the pool. The U.S. attorney’s office in Washington charged former Olympic canoeist David Hearn with destruction of property during a June 19 visit. In late July, the U.S. attorney’s office, led by Jeanine Pirro, dropped the case, citing information it had obtained that undermined “the evidentiary basis for the indictment.”

In an interview released Monday by The Free Press, Stevens said she backed the GOP candidate because “I…
articles.body:
Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) suggested former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), whom she recently endorsed for the Senate seat in Michigan over Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, could be similar to two Republican senators known to buck their party.

In an interview released Monday by The Free Press , Stevens said she backed the GOP candidate because “I think he loves the country.”

“Maybe he can be a McCain-type person or a Lisa Murkowski,” Stevens continued in the interview, referencing Sen. Lisa Murkowski (Alaska) and the late Sen. John McCain (Ariz.), two Republicans known for their independent streaks.

On Sunday, Stevens endorsed Rogers to serve in the Senate over El-Sayed, who was victorious against Stevens in a tense Democratic primary battle last summer.

Stevens’s announcement followed days of feuding between herself and El-Sayed and came only two days before Election Day.

Anger due to Israel and its war in Gaza was central to the primary fight between El-Sayed and Stevens, their recent feud and Stevens’s decision to endorse Rogers.

The House Democrat had pushed for El-Sayed to publicly condemn an anti-Israel campaign ad from an outside group. But El-Sayed refused and made it clear last weekend Stevens was not welcome at a campaign event Sunday that she had been invited to.

El-Sayed has expressed his desire for the U.S. to cut off financial aid to Israel and instead spend that money domestically. During his primary against Stevens, she received millions from pro-Israel lobbying groups.

The tension between El-Sayed and Stevens represents a broader split among Democrats over the issue of support for Israel, with many disapproving of the country’s actions in its war in Gaza, which some have labeled as a genocide.

articles.title: Who is Jason Turkish, Haley Stevens’s El-Sayed-bashing fiancé?
articles.summary: Jason Turkish, the fiancé of Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), has divided Michigan Democrats after the pair endorsed Republican candidate Mike Rogers over Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed in the state’s Senate race. Turkish’s pledge to vote for Rogers followed attacks against El-Sayed for using “antisemitic language” while on the campaign trail. “We have never seen a…
articles.body:
Jason Turkish, the fiancé of Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), has divided Michigan Democrats after the pair endorsed Republican candidate Mike Rogers over Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed in the state’s Senate race.

Turkish’s pledge to vote for Rogers followed attacks against El-Sayed for using “antisemitic language” while on the campaign trail. “We have never seen a candidate for U.S. Senate act so recklessly toward the safety of Jews in the community as we have seen from Abdul,” Turkish, who is Jewish, told The Detroit News last week.

On another occasion, Turkish told Jewish Insider that El-Sayed’s refusal to answer a question regarding whether Israel or Iran was a bigger threat to the U.S. was “100 percent disqualifying to be a United States senator.”

Turkish also pledged to attend a Rogers campaign event last week hosted by the Republican Jewish Coalition. The event — titled “Who Will Keep Us Safe? Rogers vs. El-Sayed” — featured the GOP nominee and Texas Sen. Ted Cruz (R).

Turkish is a longtime donor based in Michigan who has donated to both Democratic and GOP candidates in the past. He made multiple contributions early on to Stevens’s House campaign before she announced her Senate bid, according to Open Secrets.

According to the website, he also recently donated to Granite Values PAC , a group sponsored by Democratic Sen. Maggie Hassan (N.H.), and Dirigo PAC , a group sponsored by Republican Sen. Susan Collins (Maine), per Federal Election Commission filings.

He previously attended the University of Michigan from 2005 to 2007 alongside El-Sayed, who delivered the commencement speech the year he and Turkish graduated.

Turkish and Stevens announced their engagement following the congresswoman’s loss to El-Sayed in August. Since then, Stevens has slammed El-Sayed for a super PAC ad tying rising grocery prices to U.S. military aid to Israel.

The pair separately called on the Democratic nominee to condemn the ad, with Turkish telling reporters in late October that El-Sayed “makes my community less safe.”

El-Sayed told The Washington Post that the ad was not affiliated with his campaign, as it was run by Rebellion PAC, a political action committee supporting his Senate bid. El-Sayed said it does not speak for him, but he has not outright condemned the ad.

Turkish — who has been legally blind since birth — currently works as a managing partner of Nyman Turkish PC, a law firm focusing on accessibility issues and civil rights cases, per his LinkedIn . His work includes removing the LSAT’s logic games section and establishing an agreement for blind Michigan voters to obtain absentee ballots, according to his website .

The Michigan Supreme Court appointed Turkish to the state’s Attorney Discipline Board until September 2027.

articles.title: Mamdani’s progressive allies vie for seats in Congress
articles.summary: Three New York City progressive Democrats are expected to win their midterm congressional races in Tuesday’s election.
articles.body:
In June, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani stood before a packed house of voters, rallying support for a new wave of candidates hoping to build on his progressive momentum by winning seats in Congress.

Inside Brooklyn’s historic Kings Theatre, the crowd answered chants of “Abolish ICE”, “Tax the rich” and “Free Palestine” with roaring applause, leaving little if any room for doubt about what the audience wanted from its politicians.

Within days, all three congressional hopefuls endorsed by Mamdani – Claire Valdez, Brad Lander and Darializa Avila Chevalier – had won their Democratic primaries, becoming the party’s candidates in the midterm election.

Lander, the former New York City comptroller, defeated Congressman Dan Goldman in a race in which Israel was the defining issue.

Avila Chevalier, a community organiser, unseated longtime Congressman Adriano Espaillat. Valdez, a lawmaker in the New York State Assembly and member of Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), won the contest to succeed retiring Congresswoman Nydia Velazquez.

Both Valdez and Avila Chevalier had the backing of New York City’s DSA chapter.

The candidates’ heavily Democratic districts mean they are likely to win congressional seats in Tuesday’s midterm elections. The June Democratic Party primaries effectively served as the main event for voters.

In the final hours before Tuesday’s midterm election, New York City – a place colloquially dubbed the city that never sleeps – is more politically sleepy, with canvassers a bit harder to find than they were in the final stretch before the primaries.

For the three progressive candidates, the past few months have been a test of how to turn bold campaign promises into policy they can actually deliver. The often slow minutiae of daily governance stand in stark contrast to buzzword-laden campaign slogans on the posters and signs galvanising their base of voters.

The three congressional candidates’ platforms overlap on issues like abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), ending US military aid to Israel and establishing a public healthcare system dubbed Medicare for All. But their paths into progressive politics differ.

Lander spent years in the New York City government, most recently as comptroller overseeing the city’s finances. After losing to Mamdani in the 2025 Democratic mayoral primary, he backed Mamdani in the election.

But Lander’s congressional campaign against incumbent Goldman brought him national attention, with Israel and Palestine emerging as the defining issue in the race to lead a district with one of the largest Jewish populations in the United States.

Lander has described Israel’s military campaign in Gaza as genocide and its occupation of Palestinian territory as apartheid. He also identifies as a Zionist who embraces pro-Palestinian activism, arguing that the positions are not mutually exclusive. Lander has long supported a two-state solution.

“It’s straightforward that some approach to more shared safety for Israelis and Palestinians and for Jews and Muslims and everybody else here makes more sense,” Lander said. “I also want to be able to listen across those divides and have thoughtful policy debates.”

Two weeks before Tuesday’s election, Israeli forces detained Lander in the occupied West Bank while he was volunteering to help with the olive harvest. Israeli authorities have since revoked his travel documents for a planned return visit.

“The main story I come home with is not the story of my detention or the revocation of my travel authorisation,” Lander said. “The main story that I come with is the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in the West Bank, which I just saw with my own eyes.”

Lander has also long called for ICE to be abolished, including during President Donald Trump’s first term in office.

Avila Chevalier’s political rise was similarly shaped by immigration and Palestinian rights, though she has taken a more uncompromising approach.

After interning at a youth organisation in Nablus in the occupied West Bank in 2014, she returned to the US and became an advocate for Palestinian communities.

Her “Babies Not Bombs” platform calls for redirecting military spending, including aid to Israel, towards domestic priorities such as childcare and healthcare.

“It’s important for us to see our budgets as moral documents,” Avila Chevalier told Al Jazeera. “Our resources should be going towards the things that make our lives dignified and make our communities thrive – not towards war, not towards ICE or things that are harming our communities.”

Valdez, meanwhile, came to progressive politics through the labour movement. A former union-organiser-turned-state-assemblymember, she supports stronger labour protections, including federal legislation such as the Protecting the Right to Organize (PRO) Act to make union organising easier.

Valdez also backs national rent control and a government-run healthcare system to provide wider healthcare access than the country’s private-sector insurance model.

“Public programmes and entitlements have been under attack by the right,” Valdez told Al Jazeera as she exited a polling location in her district on the first day of early voting. “I think not just clawing those back but really advancing a vision for what those things should be will be top priorities.”

Abolishing ICE and ending military aid to Israel are lofty, ambitious goals, and neither is likely to be achieved without navigating competing interests in Congress and the White House. With the balance of congressional power potentially shifting towards Democrats in the midterms, the newcomers will have to decide which priorities to pursue first.

That means looking for more immediate wins comparable to Mamdani’s move to fill 200,000 potholes when he took office as mayor, according to progressive political strategist Nomiki Konst.

“[Get] on the same page about an issue that we all agree on and leverage that in the Democratic Congress because there’s no better time than the beginning,” Konst told Al Jazeera.

For Lander, one such measure is banning members of Congress from trading individual stocks.

“Maybe that restores a little bit of trust,” Lander said. “People say that’s gross that members of Congress trade stocks. At least this new Congress is doing something, you know, to show me they’re not just all in it for themselves.”

Lander also sees an opportunity to restore enhanced government subsidies that expired at the end of 2025, raising premiums for many people who buy their private-sector insurance plans individually.

“We can say we’re not going to pass a budget that doesn’t do that and force Republicans to vote one way or the other and see what Trump does,” Lander said.

For Avila Chevalier, an early priority would be her “Babies Not Bombs” agenda, redirecting funding towards domestic needs. Valdez wants to pass the PRO Act.

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez sets a precedent

The three would not be the first progressive New Yorkers to enter Congress promising major change.

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez won her legislative seat in 2018 by defeating longtime incumbent Joe Crowley. Since then, she has occasionally worked with Republicans on shared priorities.

In 2025, Ocasio-Cortez introduced legislation with Republican Representative Anna Paulina Luna of Florida to cap credit card interest rates at 10 percent, echoing a proposal from Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Republican Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri.

The question, Konst says, is whether Mamdani’s endorsed candidates can turn ideological commitments into legislative results. Doing so will require compromise, including setting aside some priorities to advance others.

Avila Chevalier is under the microscope after calling for New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch to resign over a man being shot in his car by ICE while his child was in the backseat. Avila Chevalier said she was later shoved to the ground by New York City police officers during protests following the shooting.

Mamdani reportedly appointed Tisch on the recommendation of Governor Kathy Hochul, whose support was important to Mamdani’s mayoral campaign. An Atlantic magazine report suggested that her endorsement of Mamdani, whose more progressive platform included universal childcare and government-operated grocery stores, hinged on Tisch’s appointment.

“Everybody wants to have their agenda passed, right? I think being really thoughtful about when to hold fire, when to fire, when to be bold, when to hold back, and when to say what you feel so you’ll get the most support,” Konst said.

But Avila Chevalier said she is willing to work with anyone to advance her priorities.

“There is always something that two people can agree on. And that’s where I plan on starting because I think organising is about meeting people where they’re at,” Avila Chevalier said.

“There are so many folks who really want to see healthcare transformed in this country, who really want to see a moratorium on data [centres]. That is a bipartisan issue for so many.”

articles.title: Trump touts DC renovations ahead of tough midterms
articles.summary: Speaking in front of the Reflecting Pool, the president went into the renovations in depth before turning to the campaign.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump started off his last public speech before tomorrow's midterms by highlighting one of his biggest second-term focuses: beautifying Washington, DC.

Speaking in front of the Reflecting Pool, Trump went into the renovations in depth before turning to the campaign.

"The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history," Trump said as he listed off his administration's accomplishments.

But even as he addressed the upcoming election, Trump returned at times to his Washington projects. Trump has turned his gaze back to the capital as Republicans face a steep climb to hang onto their congressional majorities, with voters unhappy about the Iran war and the economy.

Trump at one point acknowledged that reality, noting that "the sitting president doesn't win the midterms." But, he added, "we gave this a very strong shot."

articles.title: Why Texas Dems are forecasting a "Hispanic hurricane" in midterms
articles.summary: Two years ago, President Trump made historic gains with Hispanic voters nationwide and won a majority of Texas Hispanics. Now, Democrats believe they could s...
articles.body:
Two years ago, President Trump made historic gains with Hispanic voters nationwide and won a majority of Texas Hispanics, upending conventional wisdom and setting back the Democratic Party's hopes of making the state competitive.

They're frustrated with the state of the economy and concerned about the Trump administration's immigration policies. These factors and Mr. Trump's sagging approval ratings are giving Democrats hope in Texas' competitive Senate, House and governor's races .

"There's a Hispanic hurricane coming," said Democratic strategist and CBS News political contributor Chuck Rocha, who advises the Democratic Senate and gubernatorial candidates in Texas. "We just don't know quite yet if it's going to be Category 2 or Category 5, but it's washing ashore right in front of the GOP, and they don't know what to do about it."

But Republicans say enthusiasm for Democrats is still muted.

An estimated 39 million Hispanic Americans are eligible to vote, an increase of about 5.2 million since 2022, according to the Pew Research Center . Democrats once viewed Latinos as a built-in advantage, predicting that they'd give the party an edge and make some states competitive.

But in 2024, Mr. Trump won about 48% of the group, up 12 points from 2020 and 20 points from 2016, according to Pew's analysis of validated voters , largely for the same reasons Republicans are losing them now — the economy and immigration policy. Mr. Trump won Hispanic men by two points, despite losing them by 17 points in 2020.

The gains were even more pronounced in Texas, where Mr. Trump won approximately 55% of Hispanic voters in 2024, according to exit polling, turning blue counties in the state's Rio Grande Valley region light red.

But now, Mr. Trump's approval rating among Latinos stands at 24% , as of early October, with just 57% of Latinos who voted for the president in 2024 approving of his job performance — down from 93% in February 2025. And 51% of Latino voters said they planned to vote for a Democratic House candidate, compared to 24% who planned to vote for a Republican.

The group — which makes up more than 30% of Texas' eligible electorate — could prove pivotal in Texas' closely watched Senate and gubernatorial races.

Six in 10 Hispanic voters planned to vote for Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico over Republican Ken Paxton in an October CBS News poll . Hispanic voters favored Democrat Gina Hinojosa for governor over incumbent GOP Gov. Greg Abbott by a similar margin.

Hinojosa offered her own explanation for Mr. Trump's success with Hispanic voters in 2024 — and why they may shift back.

"The reason why Trump won, and why he was able to capture the Latino vote in the Valley and in Texas, is because he said the system is rigged – and he's right. Democrats had been defending a system that is indefensible, that is actually working against us," Hinojosa told CBS News.

She continued: "People feel betrayed. In this high-cost economy, people just want to know: are you going to work to make my life easier? Greg Abbott has been in charge for 12 years, and it is harder than ever to make it in Texas."

Mr. Trump has defended his administration's record with Hispanics.

In Corpus Christi, Texas, he touted Latinos' economic success, pointing out at a rally for Paxton and other Republicans that Hispanic American poverty fell to its lowest level in history last year, to 13.9% from 15.1% in 2024, according to the U.S. Census Bureau.

The president urged Texans to turn out for Republicans, arguing that Democratic policies would threaten the state's economy and endanger border security.

He dismisses suggestions that his support among Hispanic voters is slipping, and when asked about it, he pushed back.

"I won Hispanics," Mr. Trump said in mid-October. "I've done more than any other Republican in history. I got tremendous Hispanics."

The competing messages illustrate the political stakes for both parties in Texas, where no Democrat has won statewide office since 1994 and no Democrat has won a Senate election since Lloyd Bentsen in 1988.

The outcome could have consequences well beyond Texas. Competitive congressional districts in California, Arizona, Florida and Pennsylvania have substantial Latino populations, making even modest changes in voting preferences politically consequential.

Rocha said, "Latinos in Texas have probably moved more right than almost any state," but added that conservative, liberal and independent Hispanics are now really concerned about the economy.

"They're more monolithic than I have ever seen in my life, and they're monolithically mad," said Rocha, the president and founder of Solidarity Strategies.

Rocha said rising prices, fuel costs and affordability are driving much of that frustration — the same issues that have animated voters nationwide. Concerns about immigration policy are adding to unease among some Hispanic voters , especially in South Texas.

He mentioned a Republican homebuilder in the Rio Grande Valley who told him that immigration enforcement had frightened construction workers, making it harder to find labor and prompting him to consider voting Democratic for the first time.

But while immigration is contributing to voter dissatisfaction, he said economic concerns remain the principal motivation.

"Their first thing is always going to be prices and paycheck," he said.

In Rocha's view, Hispanics have increasingly looked like swing voters, and have demonstrated a willingness to move between Democrats and Republicans.

"It's not a realignment; it's a dealignment," Rocha said.

He says he is working on 21 congressional races nationally, including several competitive districts with significant Hispanic populations. He acknowledged that his assessment comes from his work advising Democratic candidates.

Democratic Rep. Joaquin Castro of Texas believes immigration, rather than economic concerns alone, is the principal factor behind the heightened engagement among Hispanic voters.

"I think it's mostly because of ICE and how they have targeted the Latino community in Texas and across the country, and it's the community standing up and saying enough," Castro said.

"Grocery prices are high, gas prices are high, but there have been other difficult times, economic times in our nation, and we've not seen the same kind of surge of Hispanic voting that we're seeing now."

Castro spoke to CBS News Friday, shortly after visiting the Dilley Immigration Processing Center in South Texas, where undocumented families with children are detained. He said he also visited the Karnes County Immigration Processing Center a day earlier, describing a detainee population made up overwhelmingly of Hispanic men.

He argued that Hispanic men have especially been directly affected by the administration's immigration enforcement operations.

"They feel like they've been treated like they're all criminals, and they're pushing back," Castro said. "And I think that the Republican Party is going to pay a very deep, hard price on Tuesday."

But Castro also said he's talked with White Texans concerned about how immigrants are being treated.

"It has moved people in a way that transcends race and ethnicity," he said.

Democrats have also invested more heavily in Latino outreach this cycle than in previous elections, when campaigns frequently waited until the final weeks to translate existing English-language advertisements into Spanish, Rocha says.

For instance, Talarico's campaign invested $800,000 in World Cup advertising, including Spanish-language ads, to communicate with Hispanic voters through programming they were watching.

Hinojosa's campaign ran an ad during Mexican boxing superstar Canelo Álvarez's fight against Christian Mbilli on Saturday, to try to reach Hispanic men.

Both Democrats have also worked with Latino social media influencers, including Carlos Eduardo Espina, whose online following gives them access to Spanish-speaking audiences that campaigns have historically struggled to reach.

GOP officials and their allies say they're skeptical about a shift of any significance among Latino male voters.

Daniel Garza, president of the LIBRE Initiative, a conservative Latino advocacy group, said he sees little evidence of a Democratic surge in South Texas, where he lives.

"There is no pro-Democrat enthusiasm," said Garza, who is based in Mission, in Hidalgo County. "I think most voters couldn't tell you what the Democrat plan is for bringing down prices."

Garza, a former George W. Bush White House official, argued that Democrats' outreach to Latino men in particular is unlikely to pay off in a region where many work in energy, law enforcement and federal agencies.

"I have six nephews that are border agents," he said. "You're not speaking to them."

If Democrats have an opening, Garza said, it is more likely with Latina women than with Latino men.

Ideology and religion could also play a role. Highly religious Hispanics are more likely to vote Republican , and even Hispanic Democrats tend to be more religious than the party overall, according to polling data. Plenty of Hispanic Americans also hold conservative views on issues like abortion — and while a majority of Hispanics do not approve of Mr. Trump's immigration policies, some do .

Garza also argued that Republicans' baseline of Hispanic support has risen over the past decade, leaving Democrats to fight over a narrower slice of swing voters.

"Ten, 15 years ago, the floor for Republicans was at 25%. That floor has moved up to like 35 to 37%," he said.

Referring to Rocha and other Democratic strategists, Garza said, "If everything they say is true, they should be dominating down here in South Texas."

Like Rocha, Garza sees Latino independents growing frustrated with both parties, but he believes that dynamic favors strong Republican candidates.

"I think Latinos are really looking at the quality of a candidate now, as opposed to parties," he said.

That uncertainty is reflected in recent polling.

A nationwide Pew Research Center survey found just over half of Hispanic voters — 53% — have a favorable opinion of the Democratic Party, outpacing the GOP's 29% but still highlighting the challenge Democrats may face in translating dissatisfaction into lasting support.

Early voting figures already point to heightened participation in heavily Hispanic South Texas, including the Rio Grande Valley.

Nearly 150,000 voters cast early ballots in Hidalgo and Cameron counties during the first week of early voting, a 63% increase over the comparable period in the 2022 midterm elections, based on figures reported to the Texas Secretary of State's office.

The increase is significant in a region where both parties are competing for Hispanic voters. Mr. Trump carried both counties in 2024, becoming the first Republican presidential candidate to win Hidalgo County since 1972 and the first to carry Cameron County since 2004.

The region is especially important because it's home to several competitive House districts. GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz is in a tight battle against Democrat and Tejano music star Bobby Pulido, and Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez is running against Republican Eric Flores.

In a recent interview with CBS News, Pulido described the impact of immigration policy on the district, saying "there's chaos in the streets" due to "aggressive ICE enforcement." Pro-Pulido advertisements have often focused on immigration policy.

De La Cruz also told CBS News that "enforcement should focus on the cartels and the criminals, not hardworking immigrant families." She still predicted Texas would remain red.

"But I do think that it's a wake-up call for Republicans to remain focused on affordability, and to come to a solution when it comes to immigration," she said.

Last year's mid-decade redistricting push adds another dimension. Texas Republicans made Gonzalez's district and several others redder , a gambit carried out at Mr. Trump's urging following his 2024 gains among Hispanic voters.

Those changes were designed to improve Republican prospects in several districts where the president performed strongly. But Democrats believe shifting Hispanic political preferences could complicate that strategy.

Early turnout figures indicate increased voter engagement, but don't establish which party those voters are supporting or whether higher participation will benefit Democrats or Republicans.

And Republicans caution against reading too much into early numbers.

A senior GOP strategist, involved in several House races, dismissed Democrats' optimism as "coming from the same people that have taken Hispanic voters for granted for the last decade."

"Do I think Hispanics are upset over the high gas prices? Absolutely," the strategist said. But he argued that frustration does not amount to a clear victory for Democrats.

The strategist pointed to the Rio Grande Valley's history of ticket-splitting. In 2024, he noted, Mr. Trump carried Hidalgo County even as Democratic House candidates Michelle Vallejo and Gonzalez won majorities there. Gonzalez won his race overall, while Vallejo lost to De La Cruz.

"So for all we know they could be splitting ticket down ballot even if they're coming out for Talarico," he said.

For Rocha, the larger question is whether any gains Democrats make this November can be sustained through the 2028 presidential election.

"We've now proven this is a very swingy electorate that moves back and forth," he said.

articles.title: Trump brushes aside tough midterm prospects with visit to Reflecting Pool
articles.summary: By Jacob Bogage and Nandita Bose WASHINGTON, Nov 2 (Reuters) - Facing elections that could cost his party control of Congress, President Donald Trump spent h...
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump delivers remarks at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington

WASHINGTON, Nov 2 (Reuters) - Facing elections that could cost his party control of Congress, President Donald Trump spent his last major speech before the midterms talking about pipes and paint on Monday.

Trump ruminated on his Washington renovations, new ‌sod, the White House's helipad, a grand new arch and the recently reopened Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool during a 54-minute speech that the ‌White House billed as part of the president's closing argument before voters cast their ballots.

Facing a towering marble statue of Abraham Lincoln, Trump joked he would soon rename the pool ​in his own honor rather than after the 16th president, credited with helping end slavery and preserving the Union amid the Civil War.

Trump ran through a series of pool renovations, spoke without providing evidence about vandals' attempts to damage the pool and offered updates on other projects he said would beautify the nation's capital.

"I decided to get involved in this, especially over the last few months, and we've done, I think, a really great job," Trump said.

Tuesday's elections will determine whether Trump's Republicans retain ⁠control of Congress. Nonpartisan analysts generally favor Democrats' chances of winning a majority in the House of Representatives and see the Senate as competitive.

Trump's public approval rating is now 32%, near a career low, according to the Reuters/Ipsos poll. ⁠Voters say their main concern is the cost of living. Energy prices have risen sharply since the US and Israeli war with Iran began, leaping 20% over the year prior, according to the US Consumer Price Index.

"For some reason, the sitting president doesn't win the midterms," Trump said. "But we gave this a very strong shot."

Many ​Republican ​strategists privately said they wanted Trump to focus his pitch to voters squarely on ​kitchen-table economic issues. But on a nationwide tour that has ‌included 28 rallies in 19 states since October 1, Trump has delivered lengthy asides on other topics. Those include projects ranging from a Potomac River golf course to the Kennedy Center.

The opening of Trump's more-than-$16 million renovation of the 2,000-foot (610-meter) pool was delayed by peeling paint and algae growth that turned its crystal-blue waters green. The administration defended contractors hired without competitive bidding and blamed vandalism for the issues. But prosecutors backed off the claims against a person accused of vandalism and a judge dismissed the case.

In Monday's televised remarks, Trump held up pictures of the Washington landmark as he ‌discussed the pool's new bubblers and pipework, as well as efforts to defeat algae growth. ​A new paint job, he said, "gives you great reflectivity, especially when the sun's out."

Democratic control of ​Congress would allow the president's opposition to open wide-ranging investigations of ​the president and his cabinet officials. Trump's projects on the White House grounds and the National Mall could be ripe ‌for those inquiries because he pursued many without congressional approval ​and they have faced legal challenges.

After ​talking about the pool, Trump made brief diversions into campaign substance, attacking Democrats as unfit to serve and said the US had won the war with Iran. Talks to end the war have been ongoing in recent days.

Before closing his remarks, Trump turned to other projects: ​a proposed triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery ‌and an overhaul of Washington's East Potomac Golf Links along the city's riverfront.

"We have a lot of great things planned for Washington, ​and I could get into the nation, but for that you don't have enough time."

(Reporting by Jacob Bogage and Nandita ​Bose; Additional reporting by Steve Holland; Editing by Trevor Hunnicutt and Rod Nickel)

articles.title: Actor Bill Murray stuns Trump's top economic advisor with bizarre question on news show
articles.summary: Bill Murray asked Kevin Hassett to say "my dog just died" on CNBC's "Squawk Box" to test his ever-present smile during a live interview moment Monday.
articles.body: Actor Bill Murray posed an unusual question to National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett during an appearance on CNBC's "Squawk Box" Monday morning. The "Ghostbusters" and "Groundhog Day" actor was on CNBC to promote his new six-part travel and golf docuseries "A Course Called Ireland," which premiered last week. Later in the program, Murray was invited by "Squawk Box" host Joe Kernen to ask Hassett a question. "I would regret it if I didn’t take this opportunity," Murray said. "Could you just say the words, ‘My dog just died?’ I want to see what happens to your smile." WHITE HOUSE ECONOMIST PROJECTS GDP GROWTH COULD TOP 5% AMID CAPITAL SPENDING BOOM While continuing to smile, Hassett asked, "Oh, well, is it your dog or my dog?" "Your dog," Murray answered. "OK. My dog just died," Hassett said before giving a more neutral facial expression. "We were gonna have someone go take your blood. We’re gonna call them off. Not gonna happen," Murray remarked. Fox News Digital reached out to the White House and Murray's representative for comment but did not immediately receive a response. CNBC ANCHOR THINKS CEOS ARE 'VERY SCARED' TO CRITICIZE TRUMP BECAUSE THE FEAR OF RETALIATION After the exchange, Kernen asked Hassett if he had a favorite Bill Murray movie. Hassett answered that "Groundhog Day" was a "fantastic" film and "one of the top five movies ever made." Murray joked that other political figures likely agree with him, recalling an exchange he had with former U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno about her time at the Department of Justice. "She said, 'Bill, the first thing I do to everyone at Justice [Department] is I show them that movie and I say this is what your job is going to be. 'Groundhog Day,'" Murray recalled. BILL MURRAY IS THE ULTIMATE SPORTS DAD AS SON LUKE LEADS UCONN TO FINAL FOUR AFTER DEFEATING DUKE Hassett agreed with the sentiment, likening the idea of waking up on the same day to polling ahead of the midterm elections. articles.title: How the Michigan and Alaska dramas shape the fight for the Senate: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur explains how a pair of controversies in Michigan and Alaska could impact the broader battle for Senate control.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur explains how a pair of controversies in Michigan and Alaska could impact the broader battle for Senate control. Plus, Rebecca Shabad examines President Donald Trump’s election eve message. — Adam Wollner How the Michigan and Alaska dramas shape the fight for the Senate Analysis by Sahil Kapur An “October surprise” and a “November surprise” have rocked the Senate races in Alaska and Michigan, which are critical chess pieces in the battle for the majority. To understand why these contests are so important, consider two scenarios. The “red wall” scenario: Picture this: Democrats are having a good night and hold every seat they are defending, including in Michigan. They flip North Carolina. And they accomplish their long-held goal of unseating GOP Sen. Susan Collins in Maine. That would leave Democrats with 49 seats. Other targets would include five states that President Donald Trump won by double digits in 2024: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas. There’s a plausible scenario where Democratic candidates in those states overperform by 10 points compared to the 2024 presidential margin, and still lose all of them. The “blue tsunami” scenario: Now consider this: Michigan and Maine tip into the Democratic column and, one by one, all five of the red states start to fall. The blue wave turns into a tsunami and breaches the walls of MAGA country. Through some mix of depressed Republican turnout, swing-voter movement and high Democratic enthusiasm, Democrats win Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas and Alaska. That’s their dream scenario, and it’d result in a 54-46 Senate majority. And if South Carolina flips, that’s 55 seats. The Michigan and Alaska scenarios: That brings us to two states that have sparked controversy lately. In Michigan, Haley Stevens, the runner-up in the Democratic primary, defected from her party and endorsed Republican Mike Rogers two days before the election. It’s a race where Democrats already were experiencing anxiety over progressive Abdul El-Sayed’s prospects. If Democrats lose Michigan, their path to the majority gets steeper: They would need to flip at least three double-digit Trump states, rather than two. In Alaska, a New York Times report that Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign recruited a candidate with the same name as GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan jolted the race, and the saga is under state and federal investigation. Peltola has denied any involvement in the effort. (Over the weekend, a federal judge dismissed the Trump administration’s effort to segregate ballots cast for Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher and first-time candidate.) There’s a scenario where Senate control comes down to Alaska. And if the race is close, it may not be decided for a while. Alaska law allows up to 15 days for absentee ballots to arrive, as long as they’re postmarked by Election Day, Nov. 3. That means counting can continue through Nov. 18, and the target date to certify the election is Nov. 25, the day before Thanksgiving. If it’s very close, a candidate could demand a recount. There could be a court fight. That would put the country into December without knowing which party will control the Senate. 🏃 Related read: ‘A genuine toss-up’: Senate battle comes down to red states and Republican voters, by Bridget Bowman Ahead of Election Day, Trump sets the stage for potential Republican losses By Rebecca Shabad In an election-eve speech at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, President Donald Trump said that Republicans “gave this a very strong shot,” while acknowledging that historically, the president’s party “doesn’t win the midterms.” “This is the last day before the midterm elections — the most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime,” Trump said. “The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history. These are the most dangerous candidates ever put up.” Although a White House official had said in advance that the speech would represent Trump’s “closing message” before voters make their final trips to the polls, the president spent most of his remarks speaking about the Reflecting Pool. Trump announced the Reflecting Pool will reopen after months of repairs, and talked about other renovation projects he has ordered around Washington, D.C., a key focus and fascination of his second term. Speaking about the election, the president touted what he considered economic wins. But, he said, “it all doesn’t matter if we’re going to be foolish and let people that hate our country win an election.” Trump’s speech today came after he held his final midterm rally in Kansas last night — one of 28 for him over the last month, Peter Nicholas notes. “I’m closing the sucker down,” Trump told the crowd, standing in a chilly evening breeze. “I’m getting out of here. I got to get a little sleep. I’ve been doing a little too many of these.” Read more → That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.title: Supreme Court quickly rejects Trump effort to target alleged noncitizen voters in California
articles.summary: The Trump administration alleges that about 20,000 noncitizens may be registered to vote in California, an assertion local officials dispute.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — In a loss for President Donald Trump, the Supreme Court on Monday swiftly rejected the administration’s request that California separate out up to 20,000 mail-in ballots that officials allege could be submitted by noncitizens. In a brief order without explanation, the court turned away an emergency request the Trump administration filed just hours earlier in an unusual last-minute flurry of election litigation. Lower courts had also ruled against the Trump administration. The court acted so quickly that it did not even ask California for its views first, as it normally does in such cases. California officials had resisted the Justice Department’s intervention, noting that it is already illegal under state law for noncitizens to vote and expressing skepticism about whether the federal government’s information is accurate. Separately, the administration has warned California election officials they could face prosecution if they allow noncitizens to vote. A federal judge told the Justice Department on Saturday to stop making such threats. Although elections are administered exclusively by local officials, the Trump administration says it has grounds to intervene because there is a federal law that prohibits voting by noncitizens. Trump has long claimed, without evidence, that millions of noncitizens illegally vote in U.S. elections. Experts say it rarely happens. That has not stopped the administration from putting pressure on states to check voters’ citizenship, including by using a federal database. But the effort has faced multiple setbacks. When the federal government said it had confirmed 185 noncitizens registered to vote in Nevada, the state responded that all of them were, in fact, citizens. Thousands of mail-in ballots have already been submitted and processed in California. Once election officials check whether a ballot is valid by checking the voter’s signature against voter registration records, the details identifying the voter are discarded before the vote is counted. As a result, it would be impossible to retroactively determine which votes may have been cast by the alleged noncitizens. In rejecting the Trump administration’s claims, the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals said there was no evidence Congress intended the federal law that bars noncitizens from voting to pre-empt state election laws.
